I am coming to that. In the following year we issued advertisements for tenders and we received a tender from Messrs. Petersen, Tate & Company. I may say at once to my hon. friend that the conditions offered by Peterson, Tate & Company were not very materially different from the conditions which had been gffered by the Messrs. Allan, but there was all the difference in the world in the price asked for the service. The Messrs. Allan were demanding $750,000, whereas Petersen, Tate & Company were asking only $500,000. That was a consideration, and a valuable one which could not fail to make an impression on parliament and the government. I am bound to say, that in the light of events which have taken place since, Messrs. Petersen & Tate were over-sanguipe in offering to take the contract for $500,000. It has turned out that they were sadly off in their calculation. They were young, energetic, enterprising, and it is due to them to say that they were very near succeeding, relying on their activity and their enterprise. There is reason to believe that they would have brought the contract to a successful issue, but it is a matter of public notoriety that they met with tremendous opposition in some quarters, and they had to abandon the project. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) refers to a telegram sent to me by my friend (Mr. Fielding) to Toronto in the fall of 1897, in which he announced that Messrs. Petersen & Tate had deposited the sum of $50,000 as an earnest of their intention to perform their obligations. I announced that, and I1 was glad to announce it, to the audience in Toronto. The announcement perhaps was received with great joy, and there was reason that it should be so received. I cannot see the point in the joke of my hon. friend that the announcement that their deposit had been returned, should be received with vociferous applause on the other side of the Atlantic. On the contrary, if there would be any feeling about it at all, it should be a feeling of regret, and I would have expected that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) instead of indulging in harsh criticism, should have considered it a matter of deep regret that the Messrs. Petersen & Tate had not been able to implement their contract. It was in 1899. I think, that Messrs. Petersen & Tate abandoned their contract. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) says, that from that time until 1903 the government has done nothing, has called for no tenders, has entered into no negotiations to carry out the enterprise which had been set forth in a solemn compact before parliament and the country. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is mistaken, as I will show. I admit that from 1899 to 1902, the government of Canada did nothing to try to create this Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
fast Atlantic service. But there was a very obvious reason for that. ' The paramount reason was, because of the existence of the Boer war for three years, 1900, 1901 and 1902. I would not say that that war demoralized the shipping world, but I do say that it so absorbed all the marine and naval resources of the British empire, that every one must acknowledge it would be absolutely impossible to launch the scheme then with any chance of success. It would have been folly to attempt to do anything towards the establishment of a fast Atlantic service under such circumstances. The Boer war came to an end in the middle of the summer of 1902. It so happened that in the summer of 1902, four of the Canadian ministers were in England for the coronation ceremony, and the ministers who were in England had several negotiations with different parties in order to secure this fast Atlantic service. We received a tender from the Canadian Pacific Railway, we received a tender, if I remember right, from the Messrs. Allan, from Sir Christopher Furness, and from Sir Alfred Jones. All of these tenders were of such an excessive character as regards the amount asked, that it was not deemed possible to ask parliament for their confirmation.
May I ask my right hon. friend if these tenders were laid before parliament ?

I cannot say at this moment. I am sorry my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here to answer that, but if they have not been laid before parliament there is not the slightest objection to bringing them down, and I shall be glad to do so immediately, if my hon. friend desires. But I may say that if my hon. friend had seen these tenders he would say that the amount which was asked for such a service was-I will not say excessive, but it was very large ; so large that we thought it advisable not to accept any of them, until we had made another effort to get another service. Therefore, in the month of March last, we again issued invitations to the public for tenders. On account of the excessive subsidy which had been previously asked, we thought that we would vary the character of the service, and so we asked for two boats of a very extreme speed, and for two boats of a moderate speed. We asked tenders for two boats of 21 knots and for two boats of 16 knots. We received two tenders-one of which may be dismissed at once because it did not comply with the terms-the other tender came from the Messrs. Allan. For such a service as that, limited as it was to two fast boats and to two boats of moderate speed, the Messrs. Allan asked no less a sum that $1,500,000. We did not think that we would ask parliament to ratify a contract for such an excessive amount. When I use the word ' excessive,' I do not mean

to say that it is excessive as to the value of the service which was to be given, but it certainly is excessive in comparison with the appropriation for the purpose which was made by the Canadian parliament. The appropriation which was made by the Canadian parliament was for the sum of $750,000. The amount voted never went beyond that sum ; and we cannot have such a service as is contemplated by the motion of my hon. friend even for twice that amount. We can have only a service which is partly fast and partly not so fast-two boats of 21 knots and two boats of 16 knots. To obtain a service of four boats of 21 knots, I do not know how large a subsidy we would have to ask for ; but 1 think it would be very much larger than the sum asked for by the Messrs. Allan for the mixed service. Under these circumstances, I think nobody will blame us if we do not ask parliament for such an appropriation as would be necessary to carry out the tender of the Messrs. Allan.
Now, X have only this to say to my hon. friend. In my speech in Toronto I said that the service we contemplated would not be equally popular in all parts of the country. When I said that, I only uttered a truism. There are certain sections of Canada where the advantage of the service has not impressed itself so deeply as in other parts. But my position on this subject is what it has always been. I think a fast Atlantic service would be of extreme advantage to Canada ; it would advertise the country as few other things would ; it would develop 'our trade and procure us a trade which we have not at present, but which we ought to have. I do not know how popular such a service would be in winter time. It might or might not be popular on account of the speedy crossing of the Atlantic. As a rule, all men dread the sea ; as a rule, all men have good reason to dread the sea. From the moment a man puts his foot on board the ship, he wishes to reach the other side. The passage could be accomplished iu five days instead of six of in four days instead of five, the line that would accomplish such a miracle as that would be the most popular of all lines. In summer time I have no doubt the route by the St. Lawrence would be most popular, and would be largely taken advantage of by people wishing to cross the Atlantic. Starting from Montreal or Quebec, you would have twenty-four hours or thirty-six hours on the waters of the St. Lawrence, which certainly would be a pleasure, and a good preparation for the rougher passage of the Atlantic. There is reason to believe that such a line would be patronized not only by Canadians, but by Americans, especially those from the western states. But the difficulty is to convince naval men of the profitableness of such a project. They are supposed to know the conditions of trade far better than any of us ; but even in the face of this project they have hesitated to invest their 444
money without receiving a very large guarantee from the Canadian government.
My hon. friend has also referred to an article which has appeared in a newspaper of this city which is friendly to the government, but which is in no sense an organ of the government, because the government has no organ. The government speaks for itself, and that is the only way in which a government should be represented. There are, however, papers which are friendly to the government, and the one my hon. friend referred to is one of these. But there is no reason for saying that no project for the creation of a fast Atlantic service is in existence. On the contrary, this is a subject which is always present to the minds of the government, and is always engaging their attention. At this very moment they are negotiating with some companies which have tendered for the service ; but we have nothing tangible to present to parliament at this moment. But the project has not been abandoned, and in my opinion it should not be abandoned until it is carried to a successful conclusion. Though our efforts in the past have not been successful, there is reason to hope that at an early day we shall have a tender which we may be able to place before parliament.
There is one reason why naval men hesitate to engage in this enterprise except at the cost of a very heavy expenditure by the national government :	That is, as my
hon. friend knows, coming as he does from a maritime city, that there is perhaps no kind of industry which is to-day subject to greater changes than naval architecture. Almost every year some new methods are invented, some new designs brought forward, which tend to change naval architecture to such an extent that the ship of today may be obsolete five years hence, Even at this moment, the new ships for crossing the Atlantic are being built on what is known as the turbine system, a system from which great expectations are entertained. If this experiment proves successful, we may have a new development in naval architecture which may result in all the ships of to-day being discarded two or three years hence. For this reason the very naval men who might be expected to go into this enterprise have hesitated to do so except at a cost which I think the Dom- . inion parliament would sustain the government in not incurring. When no less a sum than $1,500,000 is required to obtain a contract it is no wonder that the govern-men should have hesitated, and should have asked for more information before coming to a conclusion. I think that is a sufficient reason, in the eyes of all men who believe in economy not only in words but in deeds, for holding the government free from the censure which my hon. friend endeavoured to cast upon it.

The right hon. gentleman has, I presume, made

tlie best defence tbe government can offer for their conduct during the last nine years in connection with this feature of their policy ; and it would be quite sufficient, I think, to allow it to go to the country alongside of the speech made by the hon. leader of the opposition, and leave the country to judge of the force of that defence. But I think it is important to draw attention to some of the observations made by the right hon. gentleman. He says we have reason to hope that we may have a tender at an early day. Well, all I can say, in reply, is that the country, like the government, have been living in hope, but they have been obliged to fall back in despair. Their first hope was that they could obtain the same service for the country as was proposed by the previous government, and that they could save to the country $250,000 a year. They were sure of that, if it were only taken hold of by competent men. They said that competent men had made an offer to make a contract to that effect; and with great exaltations and blowing of trumpets, it was said :	See what business men can
do compared with unbusiness men ; we have secured for the country a service which was declared to be so desirable, so important and so advantageous, for $250,000 a year less than our predecessors contemplated. On the strength of that we have been living in hope ever since. Speaking of tenders recently received, the right hon. gentleman said the lowest tender of Messrs. Allan & Company was $750,000 above their tender of 1896. Does not that of itself show the folly of the government in not having accepted the tender made in 1896, and in declaring that it was entirely too high ? Experience has proved that they were not men of foresight, wisdom or good judgment, or they would have accepted the offer of the Messrs. Allan, and we would have had the advantage of the fast service we all desire, and besides have had that advantage at $750,000 per year less than we can get the same service for to-day.
What was the offer of Messrs. Allan & Company in 1896 ? What did they offer and stipulate to do ?

They stipulated to give a fast Atlantic service, on practically the same lines as Messrs. Tate, Petersen & Company, for $750,000 per year paid by the Canadian government and a' subsidy by the imperial government as well.
They could not know that Tate, Petersen & Company were going to offer a few years later. Tell us what the Allan Company offered to do.
Does the hon. member know the offer made by Tate, Petersen &-Company ? The offer made by the* Allan Company was practically on the same lines. They made an offer in some respects

slightly differing from the request made by the government for the service. It differed with regard to stormy weather and matters of that kind. They were not to be compelled to keep up the speed in case of snow storms or ice blockades, &c., and under certain conditions, they were not to be compelled to make the service as fast as the maximum rate. Practically their offer was on the same lines as were proposed by the government to Tate, Petersen & Company when the contract with that firm was entered into. But the government, for reasons best known to themselves, refused to recommend to the Governor General the carrying out of that contract, and defended their conduct by telling the Canadian people that they could get an equally good service for very much less money. Then they announced that they had secured an equally good service forf $250,000 per year less money, and boasted that in this they were carrying out their principles of economy and showing their great ability as business men. They said that they had not only received an offer but had actually entered into a contract, because the forfeit which was to be put up as guaranty that the company would keep its engagements was put up. Experience has proved, however, that in their conduct of this business, they were anything but good business men.
In reply to the charge made by the leader of the opposition, that since 1898 no effort has been made by the government to obtain a fast service, the right hon. gentleman said that the government had received a tender from the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1902. Why was not that information given to parliament ? Why was parliament left in the dark. Why was not this tender put upon the Table 7 We know that that attempt failed because 'if it had not, we would have had its success heralded by a great flourish of trumpets. The right hon. gentleman has told us that the South African war prevented anything being done because the steamships were all busy; but had the government ratified the contract which was made in 1896, what an advantage would not that have been to Canada during the South African war? These hon. gentlemen, however, refused to ratify that contract, and the result is that Canada has suffered very much and we have no fast service to-day.
The right hon. gentleman said that the Allan Company did not tender but made an offer. That seems to be a distinction without a difference. They offered to do the work for a certain sum. Is that not a tender ? A tender is only an offer. They offered, upon certain conditions, to do the work, and had their conditions been accepted-and they were just as favourable as those entered into with Tate, Petersen & Company, we have reason to believe that Canada would have enjoyed the advantage of a fast Atlantic service during the last

seven years at least. But the right hon. gentleman says :	Oh, we are not the only
parties who have failed; the Conservative party twice in six years endeavoured to secure that service. Yes, they did, and the first time they endeavoured to secure it for $500,000 per year. In this endeavour they failed, but when they tried to get it for $750,000 per year, they succeeded. Is my hon. friend like the Bourbons, who forget nothing and learn nothing. What is the best school in the world ? It is that of experience. But the right hon. gentleman evidently is not disposed to profit by the lessons, otherwise he would have known that when his predecessors failed to get that service for $500,000 per year, he was not likely to get it for the same price. But his predecessors were wiser than he in this respect, that they were prepared to give $750,000 per year; and had the hon. gentleman ratified what they did, we would have had a fast service for a much cheaper rate than we can obtain' it for to-day.
He began by saying that the opposition often complain that the government spend too much, but that now we complain that they are not spending enough. Our complaint has never been that the government have spent too much on a fast Atlantic service. We have backed up every effort the government has made ; we have assented to everything that seemed at all reasonable or seemed to offer any hope of success. We have never found fault with their expenditure in carrying out this great project. But we have criticised, and justly criticised, this government, which came into power declaring to the people that economy was the main plank in their platform, when we found them wildly extravagant in lines which yield no return to the country.
Let me briefly refer to the various offers that have been made for a fast Atlantic service. The government of Sir Charles Tupper received a proposal from the Messrs. Allan In 1896 which they practically accepted. With regard to some details it was incomplete, but those details could easily have been arranged, and, in the main, the offer was practically accepted. The Allans agreed to furnish a twenty-knot service for a subsidy of $750,000 a year in addition to the subsidy offered by the imperial government. Had this government advised the Governor General to ratify that contract, I have no doubt that Canada would have been in the enjoyment of all the advantages which would accrue from a fast Atlantic service. But they did not see fit to do so. On March 24th, 1897, this government entered into a contract with Messrs. Petersen, Tate & Company for a fast Atlantic servoce for $500,000 a year. One year later they had that contract amended. And what was the reason given for amending the contract ? Of course, when the contract was not carried out, the oppo-4444
sition complained of delay ; and, in answer to those complaints, the government said that they had secured the same benefits to Canada for $500,000 that their predecessors had proposed to pay $750,000. They said the fast Atlantic service was an accomplished fact. But a year elapsed and there was no evidence of the contract being fulfilled. Then the government came to parliament and said that the contractors had asked for delay, that there had been a great strike in the old country, an upheaval in the labour world, and the. contractors had not been able to carry out their contract. It was only reasonable, they said, that we should give them greater latitude. And there was another reason. There had been a remarkable improvement, they told us, in the kind of ships likely to be used for a fast Atlantic service in the future, and this firm would take advantage of that Improvement It was called the bottle-necked steamer. This was said to be the steamer of the future, and the government said they desired to take advantage of this latest improvement, so as to give to Canada the best that the progress of the world afforded. They said : Though there has been delay, that delay will result in benefit to the people, for we shall get what our predecessors could not get in their time. And the late Hon. Mr. Dobell expatiated on the great advantages of the bottle-necked steamers and what they would do for Canada, and told us that in comparison with the advantages to be gained, the delay of a year was nothing. On April 3rd, 1898, the contract with Messrs. Petersen, Tate & Company was extended, and it was amended so as to provide for the payment of $750,000 a year-not $500,000 as in the first instance, but the same amount as was proposed to be paid by their predecessors. Against this increased amount, just as against the delay, they placed the advantage that would accrue to Canada from having in this service the bottle-necked steamer, ' the steamer of the future.' It was declared by Sir Charles Tupper, when that contract was announced, that it would never be carried out. The government asserted that it would be carried out; they said they knew these men, that they were men of great financial strength, men of great enterprise, ability and experience. And they said, moreover, that these people had put up a forfeit, which the government would not hesitate to take if the contractors failed to carry out their contract. This, Mr. Speaker, was in 1898. We have no fast Atlantic service yet. These contractors applied for the return of their forfeit, and it has been given back to them, with 3 per cent interest from the time it was placed in the hands of the government. The government failed to get the fast Atlantic service for $500,000 ; they failed to get it ror $759,000 ; they failed to give us the new boats; and now we have to fall back upon the same service

that has existed for the last thirty-five years, neither better nor worse. The government, in the face of these facts, have been obliged to acknowledge failure. And now some of their organs are saying that we do not need a fast Atlantic service, that a fast service is only needed for passengers, but that what we need is a freight service, and a freight service may be a slow one. Is it the fact that we do not need a fast Atlantic service to-day ? We are living in a fast age. If two railways run from one great city to another, and one railway can land its passengers in two hours less than the other, the people will take the fast road, and freight will be sent by the fast road. In our age the individual, the firm or nation that succeeds is the one of life and enterprise, while the other must fail and admit failure. -Compare us with the United States, and where are we ? They have steamers crossing the Atlantic in four and a half and five days, while ours average nine days. Will not the people travel by -the fast line ? And will not freight follow the fast line ? Canadian mails, Canadian freight and the travel to and from Canada go by the -New York line. We need a fast Atlantic service as much as do the American people ; and to the extent that parliament fails in securing it, we fail to do our duty as representatives of the Canadian people. What does it mean to us to-day ? It means that every passenger coming to Canada is landed in the great metropolis of New York. Thousands who intend to come to Canada never reach this country at all. They drift across to San Francisco, and by that way to the Orient and never see Canada. But how would it be. if we had a fast Atlantic service ? That traffic would -come to Canada, would cross our whole country, and would take the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers at Vancouver for the Orient. We should have benefits that we cannot possibly get to-day, because the people never reach our country at all. Our mails are carried by way of New York,. And by whatever way the mails are carried the commerce will be carried. If a man in Toronto orders goods in England he asks to have them shipped by the first steamer. He wants the goods at once. Is it to be supposed that he will have them sent by a steamer that will cross in nine or ten days, when he can have them sent by a steamer that will cross in- five days? Not at all. He is a live, enterprising man and he is going to have those goods on his shelves at the earliest possible moment. To do that he must take advantage of the steamer that will cross the Atlantic in the shortest possible time ; therefore the goods will go by New York. It is the same with passengers and mails. To-day we are denied the advantages of a fast Atlantic service, which we believe we would have had if the present government had been capable, enterprising business men who would have Mr. SPROULE.
been able to grasp the situation and who would have ratified, as they should have done, the contract that was made with Messrs. Allan & Company in 1896. Every man, whether he is a Conservative or a Reformer, admits that we require a national policy in Canada, that we have a national policy in Canada which while it may not be carried out in its entirety is still the policy that Canada wants, a policy that is keeping the market of Canada for the Canadians. We want to develop that national policy to its fullest extent. We will never have the full complement of that national policy until we extend It to our transportation system as we now apply it to keep the home market of our country for our own people. We want a fast Atlantic service to assist the national policy in enabling Canada to develop her trade to the fullest extent, to do her own trade and to provide conveniences for the travelling of her own people, to carry her own products from country to country, advertising her productiveness and doing everything to show the world that Canada can live within herself and is quite as enterprising as the United States or any other country. If we consider the case of a man -coming from Europe deciding whether he should invest his money and settle in Canada or the United States, he will have submitted to him that one fact that the Americans supply a line of steamers that cross the Atlantic in five days while the Canadians take nine. What would this suggest to his mind ? That the one are a live enterprising people and the other a slow people lagging behind in the race of life. That must be the inevitable consequence of our lethai'gy in this matter. It must lead to failure in competition with a mo-re -enterprising rival, and the result is that in nine cases out of ten such a man would decide to make his investment in the country that shows life, enterprise, ability and progressiveness. We are told that we do not want this service ; I say we do want it. It is said that we may want it for passenger traffic and for mails, but not for transporting the produce of our country. The great difficulty we have to-day in transporting the perishable products of Canada so as to lay them down in a proper condition in the markets of England is the -lack of an adequate transportation service. What is needed is a faster transportation service so that these products can be laid down in a shorter time and in better condition. That would mean a better trade, larger profits, more successful operations in life, to the producers of these goods and therefore this line is of as much importance, if not of more importance, to the farmer as to any other class of the community. They are to-day losing a profit which * should accrue to them, on account of the lack of proper transportation facilities. Then the merchants of the country require this service. In order to compete in the race of life with the Americans

they must be alive to the necessities of the situation, and they must be able to bring their goods as quickly to Canada as they [DOT]can be brought to New York, and they must be able to send their mails by Canadian routes as quickly as the American mail can be sent. We must be able to give our trade to our own steamships, to live within ourselves as the Americans do. Our merchants require a fast Atlantic service just as much as do the American merchants. Then the travellers of the country require it: if we had such a service they would go by our routes Instead of through the United States, and Canada would have the benefit of an advertisement which she could never secure in any other possible way. If we were able to compute the number of people who have started out with the intention of visiting Canada and looking into her resources with the hope of making Canada their homes, but who are to-day in the United States owing to'the inadequacy of our steamship service, we would have a significant lesson as to the necessity of such an improvement, and that condition must obtain so long as we have the present inadequate service. The Canadian people must hold the government responsible for this failure. Why have they failed ? I am afraid the Canadian people will say it is because of incompetency, of inability or want of foresight and of good judgment, because if they were possessed of those qualifications we would not be without a proper service to-day. If two men started to do a piece of work and one said M cannot do it ' and the other said ' I can do it,' the one who says, ' I can do it,' and succeeds where the other fails, shows that he lias superior ability and intelligence. In this case one party made ail effort and succeeded so far as it was possible for them to succeed up to the time that they left office. Tlie other party declared that they could do better, they failed. First they made the attempt to do better, then they attempted to do it as well, now they have attempted to do it in any way and to-day Ichabod might well be written over every effort they made. They have acknowledged failure in life and 1t is time for the country to see it and know it and I am inclined to think that when the time comes for that great body to speak they will pronounce as their verdict. in no uncertain tones that the present government, has shown incompetence in regard to this transaction at least.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that this question has been made to a less or greater extent a party question. I think the people of Canada are interested largely in this subject and that It ought not to be a stock subject of political argument between one party or another. I
think that the subject of the fast line originated with the Liberal-Conservative, party. It was used for a number of years as a sort of talisman at the elections, or before the elections, to persuade the inhabitants of the maritime provinces especially and of the rest of Canada generally to support the Liberal-Conservative party in order that they might inaugurate what they termed a fast line. They used that as a sort of a talisman, not that they had any practical scheme in view, not that they had anything definite in the construction of ships, but as something to look forward to as a result of returning the party of progress to power. This question was used to influence the public mind at an early time. I remember that previous to the election of 1887 it was alluded to in the terms to which I have referred and it was a strong factor in the election held that year. It was represented that if the government then in power were returned before the snow flew this line would be in practical operation. I ventured to predict in a', somewhat iconoclastic way that probably ten years afterwards, if that party were returned to power, the same old magnificent castles of the Allan Line would be running and conveying the mails and I think I have reason to believe that I was a true prophet. As far back as 1887 the consummation of this scheme was declared to be immediately at hand. This party pledged to the consummation of the fast line, that they declared to be immediately in the foreground with such flattering prospects of its being carried out, allowed this magnificent project to remain literally glittering in the air until they went out in 1896. Then the subject came in very conveniently. At a public meeting the inevitable telegram came down that a contract had been entered into by the leader of the government with the firm of the Allans Insuring the consummation of this scheme. That had its influence no doubt. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) who has preceded me, alluded to this contract. He referred to it as if it were a definite, well arranged contract entered into on both sides, binding, covering all the essential elements and one such as could have immediately been carried into effect by their successors who unhappily interrupted the even flow of all these benefits.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) would allow me, I did not represent it as a contract that was agreed upon by both sides, but an offer which that company had made, to do this s ervice upon terms which were acceptable to the then government, and would have been entered into provided they had remained in power.

I understand perfectly what the hon. gentleman says. I also perfectly understand the difference between what he says and what actually existed. I also refer definitely to the fact that in the course of this hon. gentleman's argument

would be consumed in the voyage across the Atlantic.
Would my hon. friend allow me to ask him, is there any oceangoing steamship to-day navigated by the turbine, or any building ?

It is on the channel steamers, and I am told that the Allan Line are building a steamer with turbine engines. The turbine is also used in torpedo-destroyers, which attain an immense rate of speed. The channel, of course, is an ocean passage, the roughest in the world.
What I want to know is, has the turbine been exploited so as to be used on ships crossing the Atlantic ?
The Allans are building a steamer to run to Halifax.
It has not been tried yet; it is an experiment.

I regret that the hon. member for East Grey did not confine this subject within its own limits, but incorporated with it the question of the national policy and other matters. The construction of such ships as I have outlined would probably solve the question he has in his mind, that is, the carriage of thei more costly and delicate kinds of freight, which require the most rapid transportation. For most of the products of Canada, such as grain and cattle, the ordinary steamship would be sufficient. If we enlarge our horticultural operations so as to export grapes, plums and others of the more delicate fruits to England, fast boats would be useful; and the simplification of their construction and the diminished space occupied by the engines would enable them to carry this high-class freight. On the large steamship lines running out of New York, the principle advocated by the hon. member for East Grey has been reversed. The large passenger steamers carry the higher classes of freight, called express freight. They do not attempt to carry the bulkier articles, such as are chiefly produced in Canada at the present time. I had an opportunity of conversing with one of the highest shipping authorities in America, Mr. Bonner, freight agent of the North German Lloyds. They own the fastest passenger ships, and a large fleet of freight-carrying steamers, and also handle the largest quantity of goods of any importing firm in America. He is an expert both in the running of ships, the kinds of cargoes, the values of goods and the possibilities of continental trade. As this subject was in agitation in the House last year, I had an opportunity of getting particulars from him on this subject which may be useful. He informed me that the American manufacturers had practically abandoned to the German and other continental manufacturers the production and sale of certain Mr. ROCHE (Halifax).
classes of goods in the United States ; that notwithstanding their development of machinery, their capital, their devotion to the production of these lines, and their patriotic sentiment, that nothing consumed in America should be produced outside of America, those manufacturers were compelled to abandon to the German and other continental manufacturers the production of a certain class of goods in the production of which they could not hope to rival them. Therefore they quit the field and directed their energies upon the production of those kinds of goods which they could produce to advantage, and allowed their exchange for the goods which they imported to pay them for the loss they sustained in consequence of those goods being produced abroad. That is the policy I would commend to my hon. friend from East Grey-to ascertain by observation, analysis and discrimination, just what goods we can produce to advantage, what goods can be better produced by the manufacturers of other countries, and how much we can advantage ourselves by the exchange of the commodities which we can produce to advantage for those in which we cannot hope to rival them. I say there are great possibilities before this fast line, and the attention of Canada should be directed towards it. Without recriminations between the two parties, and without using it as a political expedient, let us all devote our energies to its consummation, derive all the benefit we can from it, and utilize it for the development of the trade in Canada and for the attraction of passengers to Canadian routes. That we shall be able to capture the American passenger trade is very problematical. There is a great advantage in having the longer rail route and the shorter ocean route ; but for some time to come the advantage of the daily sailing of boats from New York will overcome the other advantages. I think, however, that the government are now very fortunately situated, with these advantages and the knowledge they have acquired, to take up the subject of the fast line, and to enter into a contract with a reputable firm, or otherwise to acquire the means of maintaining an Atlantic passenger service as a governmental off-shoot of the great line that is projected. We do not know how many passengers will be carried, or what facilities will be given for a transcontinental and transmarine passage. All these things are in the future. We enter upon the question now at a most favourable epoch. Looking back over the history of this question, looking back to our failures, looking back to the efforts that have been made, and keeping in view the resources of our country, which are now growing so rapidly, let us at this time acquire a line which will be equal in speed, if possible, to those other lines, and at this favourable juncture project this great facility upon the mind of Canada and the attention of the world.

I would uot like, Mr. Speaker, that this debate should pass without the House giving the subject involved a full and fair consideration. It is unfortunate that it has been left to such a late period in the session, but the press of other very important matters wall perhaps furnish a very satisfactory excuse for this delay. The question is perhaps, at first view, not of such great importance to all Canada as it is to the maritime provinces, and particularly Nova Scotia ; but still I think that if it were fully discussed, and all the advantages that would result to Canada from the successful establishment of a really fast line service between Canada and the great centres of population of Europe, fully realized and understood, we would find public opinion throughout Canada supporting the government in any endeavours to realize this great improvement. I do not know7 that there is much advantage to be derived now from a discussion of the reasons why the project has so far not been accomplished. In my opinion, this matter, which had been for at least eight years occupying the attention of the late government, was in 1890 brought to a point where it might be looked upon as having been reduced to a very practical form. Stress has been laid on the fact that there was not a contract in existence between the Allan Company and the government for the establishment of this service, when the present administration came Into power. I do not think that anybody really affirms that there was a contract, but, w'e. on this side of the House, are inclined to take the view that when the administration of Sir Charles Tupper went out of office aud was succeeded by the present, matters were in such a position that the new government could have had a contract completed. Objection is taken to the conditions of the tender made by the Messrs. Allan, upon which that contract would have had to be based ; but if that be put forward as an excuse for the failure of the present admiiiis-tration, it is not one that can be successfully maintained, because the very objections that are made to the proposition of the Allan Company apply to that of the Tate, Petersen Company. The Allan Company wished for a certain delay in which to complete their arrangements. If I mistake not, they wanted a delay of four months. They further desired to have a condition inserted, which is usual with every contract dealing with business on the high seas, namely that exceptional difficulties in the matter of weather, of fog or particular moments of peril in approaching the coast, should be taken into account in estimating the rate of speed the company had to maintain. That objection could not be successfully maintained against the Allan contract, because the same objection would apply to any contract made with any company for a fast line service. But when in 1897 this matter came to be discussed in the House of
Commons and the opposition desired to know why the government had made no progress, the fact was made known that the gentlemen to whom the business had been entrusted by the present government, the late member for Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell), at that time a member of the administration, to the great astonishment of the members of this House, gave it as his deliberate opinion-and we may assume that he was also speaking the opinion of the government as well-that what he wanted was not what might properly be called a fast line service, but what might rather be called a fast freight service. If I am not mistaken, he said that what Canada wanted was a service which would give a speed of some eighteen knots per hour. The moment that announcement was made, the people of the maritime provinces felt that any such service would absolutely fail to accomplish the object we all desire. We do not want an eighteen knot service, as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said to-day. We do not pretend to say that a fast line freight service, would be an injury to the country, but what we believe is that if any line of steamers were established with an average speed of only eighteen knots an hour, we would absolutely fail to realize the advantages of our geographical position, and to call such a line a fast steamship service would be an absolute misnomer. It would uot represent properly the character of the line. Such a line would fail to realize the advantages which must be realized if we are to h^ve a really fast steamship service on the Atlantic. On account of the difficulties of communication, particularly in the summer months to the end of August, there is a point some hundreds of miles south and south-east of Cape Race, at the south-eastern point of Newfoundland, which is more or less exposed to danger from floating ice and fog. Consequently at that point there is, as it were, a corner which must be turned by all steamships plying across the Atlantic, whether going to New York, Boston or Halifax, or some port in Cape Breton or somewhere on the St. Lawrence. If a vessel is not particularly anxious to maintain a great speed, she may venture to make hef way through this portion of the Atlantic, which is more or less covered with fog, and in which floating ice may be encountered ; but if you are going to have a service of an average speed of 23 to 25 knots, it is clear that the one essential condition which must be complied with is to secure such a route across the Atlantic as may give almost absolute guarantee of security and avoid any danger of collision with ice or other vessels in the fog. To that corner, which must be turned by all steamers going across the Atlantic, the course is practically identical whether the steamers are going to Canadian or American ports The line is practically identical from that point in mid-Atlantic to the coasts of Great Britain and Ireland.

But from that point the courses of the steamers from New York, Halifax or Louisburg would diverge, and we would have from that point in the Atlantic, if we would secure the adoption of a line which would make its terminus at a maritime port of Canada, an advantage in distance which would be equal to 650 miles.
Now, 650 miles means at least a day, or considerably over a day, spent upon the Atlantic. And it is perfectly clear to the people of the maritime provinces who have looked into this matter closely that, if we l'.ave a line of steamers equally fast with the lines to the American ports in their passage across the Atlantic, the Canadian line will beat the American line by at least a day in every voyage westward or eastward. We find, then, that by utilizing the maritime ports of Canada you can land a passenger on the Canadian seaboard at least a day earlier than, he can be landed at an American port. Fortunately, the port of Halifax, the port of Louisburg and the port of Sydney are so exceptionally free from hindrance at their entrance through fog or difficulties of a tidal nature, that delays such as constantly occur at New York need not be expected or allowed for. So, with a fairly good service maintained over the Intercolonial and other railway lines in Canada, a passenger coming by the Canadian line can be landed in Toronto as quickly as he can be landed in New York coming by the American route. But to realize this advantage we must have a Canadian line that is really a fast line. We cannot do anything to divert the great volume of travel to Canadian lines, unless the steamers that are subsidized by Canada are as fast as any that ply. If we have an advantage of one-fifth in distance, we can only . realize that advantage by having steamers as fast as those of our rivals. But, if we have an advantage of one-fifth in distance and lose one-fifth in speed, it is quite evident that no outlay that the Canadian government may make will do anything to attract those for whom speed is any consideration, and so the advantage which we might hope to derive from a fast line will not be ours. Now, a fast line could not be a freight line. We cannot realize through it the advantages which the late Mr. Dobell, a member of this government, seemed to think would be realized by a line of steamers making a speed of eighteen knots. But, if we have a fast line of passenger steamers, those steamers will have a capacity of 1,000 to 1,500 tons or even more, which can be utilized for express freight and the rapid carriage of the perishable products of Canada, which are wanted in unlimited quantities in the mother country, and which, if carried across with sufficient speed, will reach the market in such a condition as to realize prices which will leave a margin for a high rate of freight. Our eggs, our

butter, our fruit, and other products, if landed in Great Britain promptly and in such steady supply as could be secured by these steamers making proper arrangement with land transportation companies throughout Canada, would be able to pay a high rate for transit of the Atlantic.
It seems to me that, while this is of the highest importance to the people of the maritime provinces, this great project is one which affects every part of Canada. We have heard one gentleman speak here today of the advantage to be derived by Canada from this project in the mere matter of advertising. That is a point which should be considered carefully, for it is of the utmost importance. Canada is so situated to-day that the two great masses of population in the world are likely, as soon as the opportunity is afforded them, to use Canadian routes as a means of passing from one to the other. The teeming population of the Asian coasts with its great commercial centres especially in China and Japan, and the great and rapidly developing population on the continent of Europe- these being by far the greatest masses of population in the world-are so placed that the shortest line of communication between them lies through Canada. That cannot be used, its great results cannot be realized, with our present means of communication. The line is practically closed to these people who would naturally make use of it, for we have not at this moment a service upon the Atlantic such as we should have, affording the shortest, quickest and most comfortable mode of travel which modern conditions provide. Give us a fast line service from Europe to Halifax, Louisburg, or Quebec in summer, and you will put us in a position to attract to the Canadian Pacific Railway and such other transcontinental railways as we may have in Canada, the most important and lucrative travel the world affords. You will practically place Canada in a position to realize all the advantages which she ought to possess from being where she is, actually on the front street of the world, the most important and what ought to be the most used line of passenger travel. There can be no question that enormous advantages would result to this country from an expenditure of anything like a reasonable amount of money which would direct the first-class through travel of practically the whole civilized world through Canada. Who can dispute that ? The advertisement to the country, the knowledge that will be acquired by those people of the highest intelligence and of the highest importance of our wealth producing capabilities in passing backwtards and forwards through this country, will be of incalculable importance to us. It would be impossible for such travel to pass through Canada constantly without disseminating throughout the world, to our enormous advantage, full information as to the cap-

abilities of our country and our sources of wealth. The two things that Canada needs, in order to overcome the disadvantage of a late start, and to place her at once in the front rank of worldpowers are population and capital. And what is more likely to give us population and capital than by placing Canada in the position to attract to herself, practically throughout her whole length, all the first-class travel from the east to the west. There can be no doubt as to the character of the advertisement we might get and as to the advantage to our country which would be made accessible to the people of the whole world in consequence of such movement. X think that, as a rule, the people of the maritime provinces were anxious to see this scheme realized and looked upon it as one of the works that the government must undertake and carry out at an early day. But X think that they realize now that no fast line that is not really a fast line would be acceptable. They do not want any substitute offered to them. We must have a line that is quite as fast and quite as good as anything to be found plying to the ports of the United States. With the work accomplished of giving Canada such a line of steamers as is to be found to-day plying between the ports of Europe and New York, we shall, no doubt, find that it has been the wisest and best expenditure this country has ever made.
Now, there has been a great deal of discussion as to the ports which should be used. It is held by a great many people that in summer the terminal point should be Quebec and that in winter Halifax or some port on the Atlantic coast should be used. That is a matter which it is not necessary at this moment to discuss, and it would be a great misfortune if the discussion of the relative advantages of the different ports should be permitted to delay a settlement of this question. The question of terminals is one that will settle itself as soon as we have the fast line. When that line has been in operation for one year the practice and1 experience of that year's operation will satisfactorily and forever settle the question of the right port to be used by such a line. What is wanted is that the government should endeavour to realize all the advantages which would accrue to Canada from such a service and should endeavour to procure them for Canada at the earliest possible moment. One argument which has been advanced here two or three times to-day has been of a most unsatisfactory character; that is, the attempt that has been made to show the advantages that come from delay, through not proceeding too quickly. It has been pointed out over and over again that if we had proceeded to complete the contract in 1896 as it was submitted to the government we would have had a service whieh, in view of what has been accomplished since that time and of what is now being done, would be an inferior
service, that the 18 or 20-knot service which would have been established in 1896 would not be equal to the service of 23 knots which we see on the Atlantic to-day, and that we would be, to a certain extent, committed to and involved in a line of steamers which would be slower than the best, and therefore not exactly what we want. That is a line of argument which, if applied at all. would involve us in a constant course of delay, and would induce us to go on from year to year without action. It would induce the government and the people of Canada to delay forever coming to a conclusion on this matter because the advances of the next year might render the best that we could now obtain inferior, owing to tbe rapid progress that is constantly taking place in matters of this kind. We cannot afford to go on forever without progress because progress is being made all about us; we must have at once a service that will enable us to realize the advantages of our geographical position and the advantages that should come to us as a rapidly growing country. The right hon. the Prime Minister to-day seemed to think that he had given an answer which ought to be satisfactory to the House and to people of Canada and to justify the government in making no progress in this matter when he pointed out that the tender submitted to the government called for an expenditure of $1,500,000. In view of the fact that this House is this session voting estimates aggregating nearly $70,000,000, it strikes me that any one who knows the importance of tbe fast line project and the advantages that would accrue from such a line, would feel that in view of the general expenditure of Canada, an expenditure of $1,500,000 for this fast service Would not be a wasteful expenditure. If we compare the present expenditure of this country with that of 1896, when the government of the day was quite ready to undertake the expenditure of $750,000 for ttoe purpose of securing this fast line, we will find that the general expenditure has practically doubled, and that therefore the expenditure of $1,500,000 for this service today would bear precisely the same proportion to the general expenditure of the country as $750,000 bore to the general expenditure in 1896. Therefore, to my mind, the cost of the service is not a sufficient reason why the government should altogether refuse to entertain this proposal. I believe and agree that they should exercise caution, and I believe, with the Premier, that economy is a good thing. In fact, I often feel that that view is not as strongly present to the mind of the right hon. the Prime Minister as it might be to the country's advantage. After all, this is a matter of enormous importance, one which involves a great expenditure, but not an expenditure which is beyond the resources of the country. It is a matter which, if the government of the country were as wideawake

as I hope to see them, and as I believe the opposition are, to the development of our industries, and particularly of our shipbuilding, they might very well utilize to induce the construction of large steamers in this country. I would like very much, when the time comes that this project is to be realized, that it should be so managed as to lay the foundation of a great shipbuilding industry somewhere in Canada, and if the government of the day were in a position to make a contract for the construction of two, or three, or four great steamships of the size and power and cost of such steamships as are now occupying the first place upon the Atlantic, they might be able, by calling for the construction of the steamers in Canada, to induce one of the great shipbuilding companies to transfer at least a portion of their shipbuilding plant from the mother country; and to establish in Canada a shipbuilding industry. It would be a most important thing to us if in addition to the fact that we have a line of steamers of the fastest speed, running over the shortest route and affording to the travelling public the greatest possible facilities in regard to comfort and speed, we could proclaim that this Canadian line of steamers, the finest and fastest on the ocean, were of Canadian construction. That would have great value as an advertisement for our country. We have had this matter threshed out in the maritime provinces. Last year a large and representative meeting was held in Halifax at which men of all shades of political opinion, men deeply interested in the commercial success of Halifax and the province, came together and in every way in their power endeavoured to impress on the government the fact that it was regarded as being of the utmost importance to the . province of Nova Scotia that this project should be accomplished. They endeavoured to put their views in such a way as to show that this matter was of importance, not only to the province of Nova Scotia and to the cities by the sea, but to the whole people of Canada. We should not expect that such an outlay as is contemplated should be made in deference to the opinion of any locality. The people of the maritime provinces do not feel for a moment that they should come to the parliament of Canada and urge upon it the adoption of the scheme involving a large expenditure if it was of a local character, and if it affected merely sectional interests. Our opinion is that we have here the shortest line of communication between the greatest masses of population in the world; that we have, if we choose to realize it and to go to the expense necessary to realize it, a position that will place us in the forefront of the world's traffic, and will develop through our country the greatest amount of travel of the most wealthy people and give us all the advantages that must come from full and complete knowledge of Mr. BELL.
our country by these people. No one who visits the western portions of our country can return from it without a feeling of amazement that the country is not making more rapid progress and development and receiving a larger population and without feeling that it is an undeveloped country. What is the cause of that ? That there is as yet no knowledge of our country possessed by the people of the world. Even if the people of the older provinces in Canada to-day have no adequate knowledge of its resources, the extent and the possibilities of wealth to be found in Canada, and if no other advantage could be realized from the establishment of such a line of steamers as I am now advocating than the fact that it would communicate to the world knowledge of our possibilities, of our extent, of our capacity for producing wealth, then I maintain it would be scarcely possible to estimate the advantage that would be derived by this country from the expenditure we have in view.
But, if iu addition to that, a mere calculation ;be made in the most commercial fashion, if we were to develop the commercial view to the utmost and look upon the extent to which shipping would be carried on by a fast line of steamers with the enormous outlay that would be made in connection with the operation of such a line of steamers, with the enormous amount of valuable supplies that would require to be purchased in Canadian ports for such a line of steamers and with the enormous aggregate of increased value which would be attached to all these products of an essentially perishable character of our Canadian farms and orchards which we are sending to the mother country in enormous quantities, and which we hope to send in increased quantities ; then, even from the most commercial point of view which it is possible to take, it seems to me that it would be quite possible to prove conclusively that this expenditure of $1,500,000 would foe repaid directly to the people of Canada in the increased wealth which would be brought about as the result of such an expenditure. There is another thing. I believe that Canada has derived in the past a great deal of credit and advantage from the fact that her conduct throughout has been, in view of her comparatively sparse population, progressive and courageous. There is no doubt that Canada has derived a great deal of advantage from the advertisement she has received the world over from the fact that though a young country, with a small population. she had the courage and ability to grapple with such enormous public works as the Intercolonial Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and to carry them to a magnificent and successful completion.
And the Grand Trunk Pacific.

mission, marks an epoch in the history of rapid ocean travel. All these things have been accomplished and in the course of a few months will be finally settled. If the Canard Company, in the construction of two new steamers, adopts the turbine engine, it may be taken for granted that the turbine engine is no longer a matter of doubt. If the result of the adoption of the turbine engine system be, as it is expected it will be by these great Atlantic greyhounds, then these great steamers, with the tremendous speed which they will develop from this new motive power, will increase their earning capacity, and one after another of the objections which may have stood in the way of the government proceeding to deal with this matter will have been removed. No longer will there be strikes, or the interference of a great war with business ; or the anticipated introduction of some new and approved method which might, perhaps, outclass the steamers which we at the moment were proposing to build. The government is now in such a position, that they will be unable to approach parliament again with any excuse for inaction or for failure to accomplish the end we have in view. They will be clearly open to the charge of being half-hearted in dealing with this great measure, if they do not, at the next session of parliament, submit some tangible evidence that we will have a fast line in the near future. For my own part I feel that this is a matter of importance to the whole of Canada, but apart from that, I feel that it is of particular importance to the maritime provinces. I know that there is no idea quite so cherished in the minds of the active business men of Nova Scotia, as that they may hope at some early day to see Halifax, or some other port in the maritime provinces become the terminus of a steamship line, which will be of world-wide fame, and which will turn to the shores of our country the most enlightened, the most cultured, and the most enterprising and energetic of the people of this world.

Earlier in the session I had the opportunity of giving my views on this fast Atlantic service, so that to-day I need not occupy but a few moments of the time of the House. I congratulate the member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), upon the fairness of his speech. He has stated his recognition of the difficulties which lie in the way of the accomplishment 1n the immediate future, of the object which we have in view in reference to this fast Atlantic service. I regret that the motion before the House after expressing the opinion that we are in favour of this project, has gone further and proclaimed a want of confidence in the government. The first clause of the motion reads :
This House affirms its belief that great advantages would result to Canada, as well as to the mother country from the establishment of a fast Atlantic service between the two countries.

Had the motion ended there, it would have been accorded the unanimous approval of this House, and it would have given strength and aid to this government in the furtherance of this difficult undertaking ; but unfortunately, the resolution goes further, and it makes a party question of a matter that ought to be above politics. Personally, I am firmly convinced of the vast benefits which would be derived from a Canadian fast Atlantic service ; but I cannot declare by my vote, that the government have been derelict in their duty when I believe that they have not been, and I know that they have encountered great difficulties, some of which have been enumerated by my hon. friend from Pictou. Let me say, Sir, that my opinion is, that if we cannot get a really fast Atlantic service, then we should not subsidize a so-called fast Atlantic ser-vince. I am opposed to subsidizing steamers of less than twenty knots. We should have a fast line in every sense of the word. I believe that one great benefit to be attained will be the advertisement which Canada will get before the world. Any one who has travelled in the old land must recognize the dire ignorance of a great many people there, as to the capabilities, the resources, and the geography of Canada. I regret to say that 95 per cent of those who come from England to Canada, come through the United States. They receive their first impressions of this continent in that great and wealthy city of New York. They enter our Dominion through the backdoor of Canada, instead of by the front door, which is to be found in the maritime provinces. The traveller when he lands at a Canadian port in the east, as he travels to the Pacific coast, learns as never before what a magnificent heritage the British empire has in this Dominion. If we had a steamship service equal to the best running to New York, we would have the travel from England diverted through Canada, and we would afford to Englishmen who came to Canada an oportunity of realizing the great extent and great natural wealth of our country. I believe, that viewed from this aspect alone, it would fully recompense us, for the granting of even a large subsidy to this service. I promised that my remarks would be brief, and I shall not enter further into an argument in favour of this proposition. I repeat, that if we cannot get a real fast line of steamers, we should not enter into competition with the private companies which are now engaged in the Atlantic trade. Let us have a fast Atlantic service in the true sense of the word ; a fast Atlantic service which will be a world-wide advertisement for Canada ; a fast Atlantic service which will be able to compete with the very fastest steamers running to United States ports.

It is unfortunate for Canada and for this parliament, that all great questions are relegated to a few moments discussion, whereas the

little petty domestic questions are dilated [DOT]on for weeks and weeks. That has been the misfortune of Canada ever since confederation. A trifling question, as to whether a little wharf should cost $5,000 or $10,000, receives days and days of discussion, but a great question which makes for the life of the nation, is thrown overboard in a few minutes. That has been the weakness of Canada, and so long as I am here I shall endeavour to correct that weakness. We want to discuss national affairs here. We want to make a nation of Canada, and we cannot make a nation of Canada by discussing, for days, five thousand dollar grants to wharfs. We cannot make a nation- of Canada by taking weeks in discussing the question of binder twine. These questions may be discussed in the township council ; this parliament is for the discussion of great national questions. It is for us to solve the problem of how we can lay the foundations of Canada, so that she may have a controlling and dominating influence in the whole world. When such a question is under discussion here, some people make excuses for the time that they occupy. I shall make no such excuse. The debate on the transcontinental railway, and the debate on this fast Atlantic line are the only two subjects which were worthy of the consideration of the Canadian parliament this session. These other petty questions, can be discussed by school trustees, and by county councils, whose members have no ideas beyond the mere parish in which they live.
Now, Sir, I want to say, that the conduct of the Canadian people with reference to the establishment of a fast Atlantic line, has been insignificant and mean beyond all compare. We have been pretending to make progress on this continent; we have been pretending to dispute the supremacy of the United States in commerce, and, yet we have been debating for ten of fifteen years, whether we are to establish a fast steamship line.
I was pleased with one remark of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell). He said, what are we engaged in these internal developments for, what are we building lines of railway for, unless it is for the purpose of carrying the commerce of this country to the sea ? And what is the use of carrying it there unless we have the most approved facilities for distributing it over the whole world ? We are always beginning things in Canada at the wrong end. We are such a little, illogical people. We have been accustomed to look at public questions from such a narrow provincial standpoint that we have not an intelligent idea in our pates about the possibilities of Canada as a whole. The time is past for that kind of thing ; and hereafter when I hear any man in this parliament endeavouring to bring the great public questions down to the low level of party politics, I
will say he is not fit to be in this parliament. The question before us is whether Canada is to be a great commercial country. What man would ever think of party politics on a question like this ? The man who would introduce politics on this question would want his mother-in-law's funeral to be run on political lines. This is a business question, and is to be discussed as such. If a great steamship or mercantile company, with the resources of Canada, wanted to establish a steamship line, it would have been established in two weeks. I think the Prime Minister ought to have blushed when he referred to the statute passed on this subject as far back as 1889 ; and I venture to say that that statute was not passed without a discussion for ten or twelve years previous. The people of Canada are so sleepy and so narrow that you have to talk about a question for years before it enters parliament; and although this question entered parliament in 1889, we find that statute after statute have been passed, and year after year has been wasted down to 1903, and we are not one step nearer to a fast Atlantic steamship line than we were on the day the first word was spoken on the subject. Is that creditable to the people of Canada ? Does it look like the action of a dominating people ? Can we ever hope, with such conduct as that, to become anything but a people who will receive the contempt of the whole world ? I think the people of Canada deserve the contempt which the people of the United States have shown to us. The public men of this country should be spat upon for the mean, contemptible way in which they have treated the people of Canada. We look to them to lead the people. Instead of that, the people have had to drive them with a whip. Instead of leading, they have been, like cowards, listening to hear what this or that little man would say. The leader of a people should have at least twenty-five years of out-look beyond the ordinary man, and then he should beckon the people to come on and follow him. Instead of that, we have had the political leaders of this country, little fellows, holding back until they have been horsewhipped by the country and forced to go on. The people have been bigger than their leaders. That has been the position of affairs in this country. I for one protest in the name of Canada. I want to see this country great. I do not want to go down to the grave with this country but little greater than it was when it came from the Indians. We hear a great deal of talk, but we have been making little real progress. We have been for fourteen years talking about establishing a fast Atlantic steamship line, which a company of business men would have established in twenty-four hours. I want to refer to one remark of the Prime Minister, and in doing so I do not wish to be unkind. I think the Prime Minister made a great mistake in talking about this question of a subsidy,

when he spoke of the difference between $750,000, which was the subsidy for which the Allans offered a steamship service some years ago, and the $500,000 for which the Tate people afterwards ottered to establish a line. Has it come to this, that on a great national question of establishing a steamship line to dominate the trade and travel of this country, a public man tells this House that $250,000 is going to be considered for one moment ? Further, the Prime Minister said, even now this House would consider very gravely this question. I undertake to say that the right hon. gentleman misstated the character of this House, Or else this House ought to be dissolved to-morrow, and a better class of men brought into it. If that statement is true, this House ought not to be permitted to represent the public feeling of Canada one hour ; because it is entirely beneath the public sentiment of Canada as it exists to-day, and the sooner it is thrown to the winds the better ; and let an able, cultivated. broad-minded class of men come in who will represent the public opinion of Canada as it exists to-day. I was sorry when the Prime Minister said that even now this House could debate about $250,000 on the great question of establishing a steamship line which might mean the dominating of the commerce of the Atlantic by Canada, instead of it pouring into New York and making that city one of the great commercial centres of the world. I want to say a word to the people, not of Ontario- I know no Ontario on this question-but the middle west of Canada, which is around the great lakes ; I want to refer also to the west of Canada, and then I want to refer to the Pacific coast of Canada. There are no provinces on a great national question of this kind ; and any man who debates this question from a provincial point of view shows that he has not got above the narrow provincial education of former days. I am not a Nova Scotian ; I am not a maritime province man. I am a Canadian, and it is my duty to advocate a harbour on Lake Superior just as strongly and ardently as I would a harbour in Nova Scotia. If I did not do so, I would not be worthy of a seat in this parliament. I want to say that this is not a Nova Scotia or maritime province matter. It is a Canadian matter, and the fame and reputation of Canada depends on the exploiting of her maritime powers. No nation in the history of the world has ever achieved greatness without being great on the sea. England was almost a barbarous country three hundred years ago, and she had to whip Spain and Holland and France in succession in order to triumph on the sea. When she did that she became the great wealthy power of the world. Spain was great when she was a commercial power. So was Holland. So was Venice when all the ships of the world sought her ports. Go back to the very dawn of time, Mr. GOURLEY.
and you will find that the nations that were great were great in commerce. We ought all to be students, and there is only one book from which men can learn anything worth learning ; 'that is the book in which human experience is put down. That book is the hook of all-history. It tells us, if we will learn, that our country, in order to be great, must master the commerce of this continent; and how can we pretend to do that unless we can establish a fast line of steamships of our own and capture the passenger traffic ? Here is the Prime Minister going over this country talking about our being a young nation, when he cannot secure the travel, when we cannot get the men who are going to London from Canada to take a Canadian steamer. We talk about being a nation, we are nothing but scrubs, and the United States people will some day wipe us off the face of this continent. I hope that these unfortunate rumours that we hear about the corridors are not true; because if they are. all the Yankees will have to do is to make a claim for Canada and they will get every square mile of it by their boastfulness and dishonest methods in diplomacy. I refuse to believe these rumours; but if they be true, we may as well give up all commercial aspirations. But if we are to have a line of steamers, that service should be the very best. It should not be inferior to any steamship service on this continent. We should have a steamship service which will rival the great New York lines. What is the sense of talking to-day about an 18 knot service and a 20 knot service ? Why not get a half a dozen of rafts and start them from Halifax ? That would be just as good as an 18 knot service. I would just as lief jump into the Atlantic and swim across as take one of your 18 knot boats. Such a proposition is an insult to the Canadian people. If you establish a service inferior to any other that exists on this continent, you will hear from the maritime provinces. We have our power in this confederation, and are not to be imposed upon by any second or third-class steamship service. Let me tell the people of Ontario that they are a maritime people and they ought to exploit, their great lakes and equip them in the very best fashion. In like manner should the people of the Province of Quebec look after their maritime opportunities. Let them equip the whole line of the St. Lawrence and the Bay des Chaleurs. That whole route should be covered with wharfs and furnished with the most improved system of securities to navigation, so that ships in distress could obtain shelter at any time and the world would know that the coast of Canada is the safest place on the north Atlantic in which to seek refuge. Then look at the humiliating position which we have been placed by the boastfulness of our Yankee friends. They have boasted us out of existence. What happened in London at

the dinner of the Pilgrims Society the other day ? Our Commissioner, Mr. Aylesworth, had to get up and tell the British people that there was another country on this North American continent besides the United States. These Englishmen, these stupid Englishmen

I speak of the Englishmen of the last sixty years. I am of English descent but of the great English breed before two generations ago. The last two generations are degenerates and cowards. They have had no leaders for sixty years. Since Pitt died, there has never been a great leader in England.
