That breed is coming back. We have it in Canada to perfection. The highest breed of the Saxon race to-day is in Canada. We have never become degenerate, but we have been overshadowed by the bluster and brag of the United States. I want to make ports in Halifax, St. John and Montreal that will overshadow New York, Boston and Portland, and we can do it. Talk about $250,000. Why, Mr. Speaker, if you are a wealthy man you should give a check and settle this thing in five minutes. Fancy the people of Canada haggling over a paltry $250,000, when considering the question of a national line of fast Atlantic steamers. No wonder we have been and will continue to be the laughing stock of this continent. One morning at breakfast last summer, I took up a newspaper and saw that a number of people had gathered to say good-by to the Countess of Minto, the beloved wife of the Governor General, and a lovely woman. But it was very humiliating to find that even the consort of our Governor General should have to leave our shores and go to a United States port to take passage for England. What could be more insulting to the high spirit and pride of the people of Canada than that the wife of our Governor General should have to go to New York to find her way to London ? I am imputing nothing or passing no criticism on that lady's conduct, but merely giving it as an illustration of the inferior position we occupy. I presume that the Governor General will do the same thing. My boy at the breakfast table asked me why this lady went by New York. That is the first question that suggests itself to the minds of the young people in this country. This kind of thing poisons the mind of the young. It tends to make them think little of their own country and to look upon Canadians as inferior to other people. Why should our Canadian merchants run to New York 445
when they want to leave this country ? I have a letter from a young man, belonging to Truro, who crossed over to England, and he says he will never go to England again until we have a fast Atlantic line of steamers. He says that over at the Cecil Hotel in London there were a number of Canadians who appeared to view this thing in a different light; but the people of Ontario have never had the national prida that we feel in the maritime provinces, because if they had, we would never have had Portland made the terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway. There would have been a revolution first, but they had their spirits subjected and their souls depressed by subjection to the United States. We have never undergone that experience or occupied that position in the maritime provinces, and consequently we cannot understand why Canadians should submit to this inferiority. This young man was in London at the Cecil hotel a little while ago, and he found that every Canadian there intended crossing the Atlantic to New York. He was the only one who was taking a steamer to Halifax, and he said that he was reviled and laughed at by 'these Canadians from Ontario, just because they were in the presence of Americans. They thought it good form to laugh and sneer at the Nova Scotian who was sticking to the route by Halifax. He would have to leave two days earlier and arrive a day and a half later going by Canadian steamers, and he said :	I wiil
never go to the old country again until we have a fast line of steamers; and he begged me for heaven's sake to urge the parliament of the Dominion to remove this humiliation which the people of Canada have to suffer in the old country when they meet a lot of Yankees who boast of their splendid fast steamship service and ridicule Canadians.
I want to refer for a moment to the excuse which the right hon. the Prime Minister gave us for delay. The Boer war has been responsible for a lot of things. Just imagine the Premier giving the Boer war as an excuse for this long delay in establishing a fast steamship service ! Why, the Boer war started three years after he came into power. It did not start until October, 1899, and he had every chance during the preceding three years to establish that service. But what discourages me more than anything else is his statement that we must wait for naval changes. Why, from the earliest time naval changes have been going on from year to year, starting with the old Greek triremes. Suppose the Greeks had waited for modern steamers what progress would they have made ? The Prime Minister wants us to wait for two or three generations until we ane all gone and will only be able to look down from a higher sphere at what is taking place here below. I know nothing that encourages me to think that this line of steamships is more to the



front, than It was ten or fifteen years ago. As to naval changes we ought to establish our steamship line now, in the best fashion that the world's development in navigation will allow. Of course, naval changes will take place. When they take place, adopt them. That is what the steamship lines do, and why should we not do the same ? To wait for naval changes, that might take place, is^fiio way to meet this problem. That is but a weak excuse that the Prime Minister gives us. I hope the government will not wait for the turbine. Of course, we all hope to see the turbine developed, and made practically useful, for it will make the passage across the Atlantic a mere holiday trip, of two or three days. That is one of the splendid accomplishments we may hope for, in the future. But it is a good deal like the wireless telegraph-it will come In two or three years, perhaps five or ten years ; but it will take time to perfect it. Do not, for heaven's sake, delay this line for any such chimera. It will come in good time, but, in the meantime, our fast Atlantic service will be established. Get the best line that can be attained, and get it at pnce. The question has been raised of an expenditure of $250,000, more or less. What is $250,000, in comparison with a scheme like this ? Let ns spend $5,000,000, if necessary. Why, you are giving subsidies to railways, half of which, no doubt, will be stolen. I have no doubt, that enough will be stolen out of the railway subsidies, given this year to give $5,000,000 for a fast Atlantic service. I have no interest in this mean economy. The people do not mind expending money. All we ask, is for you to keep it out of the hands of the boodlers. If it is spent honestly, let it pour out in a stream. We cannot do the work we are here to do, if we are to stop to consider a question of $250,000, in connection with a scheme to join the two continents, and give Canada a precedence throughout the world. Why, it is like a rich man talking about whether he will give ten cents or twenty-five cents to his valet- what does it matter which he gives ? If you are going to get the service, you must pay for it. But what has happened ? I do not want to blame the Prime Minister too much, but just think what this government of business men did. They found a contract witli the Allans, when they came into power-or an offer from the Allans. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Roche) made a point about the difference between a contract and an offer. Why, even lawyers do not think of these differences. If two men meet and agree, that is a contract-a clerk can look after the matters of detail. All that -was necessary, in this case, was for the government to say the word, and they could have had the fast line, at once. Then, if the Allans found that their subsidy was not enough, let them come back, and we could double it. If they still found it not enough, let them come back, and we could Mr. GOtTRLEY.
double it again. That is the way for men to deal with a great scheme like this, at the founding of a nation. We are not deputy reeves of a township. We stand at the creation and birth of a nation, and we must have bigger and broader ideas, if ve are to yove ourselves statesmen equal to our opportunities. And what has this penny-wise-pound-foolish statesmanship led to ? A few years ago we had an offer from the Allans for a line of steamships for $750,000. The government, inspired by Ontario politics-for I see the hand of Ontario in all this-wanted to cut this down. They wanted to go to the public and say : We have saved $250,000 ; two hundred and fifty thousand dollars ! What great statesmen we are. Why in any reasonable country they would have been hooted from the political platform. But the Prime Minister-and, living so near the Atlantic as Quebec, lie should have had a broader outlook and wider aspiration ; but I believe he was speaking in Toronto and no doubt he felt the freezing influence of Toronto around him so his ideas contracted under the chilling influence-boasted of this saving of $250,000. It is greatly to his discredit that he introduced such an argument into the consideration of a great question like this. It was beneath the dignity of the Prime Minister of this country. I say to the Prime Minister that he should not have allowed his Ontario colleagues to interfere. He should have told them to stand by while lie settled this question himself. He should have said : Go into another room and sit down until I get through with this business. But, instead of doing that he listened to them. And now, instead of accepting $750,000, the Allans come back and demand $1,-
500,000	for the same work. That is the result of this picayune policy of saving ten cents in connection with great national issues. It is something like our fellows-and I mention this to show that I have no sympathy with this kind of thing wherever it is found-who went down to Newfoundland to negotiate the bringing of that great island into confederation. They went there and they opened a bargain as if they were buying so much old junk. They thought that a great people like the people of Newfoundland should be content to deal with a matter of this kind on the basis of figuring out with the stub of a pencil and trying to cut off five cents here and ten cents there. Why, what would a proud province like Newfoundland do? They turned them out and have been laughing at them ever since. Why, in such a matter Canada's position was like that of a man courting a girl. He may cover her with diamonds but when he marries her they are all his own. Whatever we had given to Newfoundland would have been ours after the union. But these people had not outlook enough to see that. So are our dealings with this fast line subsidy.
Now, with reference to speed, I want

first to know the speed to New York, and I want to have a line that will be one or two knots faster. It is idle for us to enter into a contract with steamers having the same speed as those to New York. That port has its advantages. It fills the mind, it fills the imagination of the world, and it will be attractive above the ports of Canada even with the same service. You have to establish in the public mind of England and Canada the fact that the service to Canada is faster than that to the United States. Therefore, I repudiate any service unless it is faster by one or two knots than that to New York. I want no more picayune, tu'penny-ha'penny bargains. Either throw the project up and say we are not equal to it, or establish it whatever it may cost. As to the port to which it is to run, let these competent steamship people determine where that is to be. We can control them, whether they go to Quebec, Halifax, Montreal or St. John. Pile on the subsidy; give them every help that they need ; let Canada settle this question, once for all, whatever it may cost. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) referred to the ignominy endured by the people of Canada, from the fact that the English parliamentary visitors coming to Canada, landed at New York. Of course, that is a back-handed slap at Canada. It is an advertisement to the people of Europe, and to the world, and an acknowledgment on the part of the people of Canada, that the people of the United States occupy a superior position, and we an inferior position. And that is the idea that prevails. There is ho use talking about it, it prevails. The result is that to many of the English people, America is the United States. And we deserve that. Do not let us shirk our responsibility ; we are responsible for the opinion that exists in England because we have allowed the port of New York to be known all over the world. New York is in the United States and most people in the old world know of no port in America but the port of New York. That is America to them, and although we have ports here, we have stood by and let them remain unknown, and as a consequence Canada is unknown and we are responsible, we who are sitting here in parliament are responsible for the degradation of Canada, and we cannot escape that responsibility. I am determined, as far as I am concerned, to escape it; if you want the degradation, you shall have it, but I shall have no part of it; I shall declare to this House and to the country that we alone are responsible for the fact that Canada occupies the mean position on this continent she occupies to-day. Halifax, St. John and Montreal should be more than equal to Boston or New York if we had had men equal to Henry Clay and Daniel Webster who exploited the national resources and national fame of the United States. But we had a smaller class of men, or if we had some big men we had so many small men 445J
that they climbed on their backs and kept them from carrying out their ideas. Of course the Liberal party are more .responsible for that; the hon. gentlemen were chiefly concerned whether napkins should be washed once or twice a week, and whether a gentleman should have more than one champagne glass for each of his guests. These were the great questions that occupied the attention of parliament year by year, when these great topics to which I have referred should have been up for discussion. With regard to the term for which the contract should endure, some gentlemen say you should make this contract for ten years. That is too short. How can you expect a great company to invest millions of money on a contract that will run for only ten years ? You can scarcely get a great enterprise started inside of ten years. You should make your contract for a long period and in a liberal spirit, so that the company entering the contract would know from the start that they were in the hands of sympathetic friends, of people who desired to help them at every turn and not to worry and harass them. We should make a contract for twenty or thirty years in order that the company may feel sure of a safe and growing business and that no shortness of time would deprive them of the advantages they might expect from the exploitation of their business, and that no other company should be able to come in and for some little question of a million and a half dollars of subsidy cut their trade from under them. What a tremendous thing it would be for Canada to have a powerful company go into this business and exploit it! Equip your ships with the greatest luxury and comfort so that they will be superior to anything in New York, and then if necessary, build one or two short lines from here to Halifax or St. John, and make your coaches and dining cars on these lines the finest in the world, so that every man from England or any European country returning from New York would say :	The finest railway and steamship service In America is the Canadian service. Let us spread that idea abroad whether it costs one million dollars or ten million dollars and then we shall have done something for Canada. Would it not have been better fifteen or twenty years ago to have grasped that idea and to have borrowed $20,000,000 for this purpose? It might have given us thousands of millions of a return, given us population, gixen us fame and reputation and lifted us from the petty position of little provinces into a great nation. The only way in which we will ever get to be a nation is by adopting comprehensive measures of this kind. Sir, I am the smallest man in the county of Colchester, the man with the most limited vision, with the narrowest ideas ; my constituents are all my superiors in education, intellect, brain and everything of that kind, and therefore I am surprised when I find

a number of members of parliament up here who seem not the equals of the average citizen of the province of Nova Scotia. X expected when I came to this parliament to see men of vast learning, and vast outlook, and vast research, and vast capacity for statesmanship. There are such men in Canada and perhaps there are such men in this House, but they have not exhibited that liberality and breadth of sentiment in this matter that I could have desired. 1 hope the time will come when in discussing matters of this kind men from Ontario and from Manitoba will'be the first to rise and say :	This is a maritime question, let us
join together to further it. A maritime question is really more important to a man in Manitoba or the inland country than to the people near the sea, because what is the use of people in the inland provinces raising vast crops if they have not the easiest communication to the sea and the best communication across the sea to carry their products to the markets of the world? I hope that hereafter we will not see maritime province members indulging in these discussions ; it is wrong-gentlemen from the west, from Ontario, should be the first on their feet to urge the claims I have been urging to-day. That I hope will be the character of the public men in this country in a few years. If the question under discussion has reference to a harbour at Midland or on Lake Superior it will be the men from the maritime provinces and the men from British Columbia who will support it. It will be these men who will urge the opening of communication with the western prairies via Hudson's bay in order that the grain of the west may reach Europe by that route instead of dribbling south through the United States. That should be the ambition and the hope of every man in this country, and, so far as I am concerned, I will never cease advocating these opinions because until we accept them we can never be anything but little, scattered and disjointed provinces.
Hon.. Wm. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Mr. Speaker, I protest against the expression which my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has used in reference to the want of intelligence of the Englishmen.
I meant those of the last sixty years ; of the last two or three generations.

Let us take the House of Commons and the House of Lords in England to-day and you will find there representative men equal to any House in Europe or any other place, and it would be well for us, and well also for the hon. member for Colchester, if he had the intelligence and the logical acumen that these people possess. Certainly they would not wander from Dan to Beersheba as the hon. gentleman has done.

That is the trouble with them ; they have blinders on and never see Mr. GOURLEY.
anything between these blinders. God help my soul there is not one of them fit to drive a band of sheep across the country.

I am pretty well acquainted with the people of Colchester county of both parties, and I must say I do not know one man of either party in Colchester county capable of making the speech which we have listened to from the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) to-day. He and I agree on one thing, that the fast line should be kept out of politics, and that both parties should unite in securing the fastest and the best service, and I think it is a most fortunate thing for the Dominion of Canada that we did not engage in a fast line eight or nine or ten years ago, because if we had done so we would now be behind the age in every respect. While the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) condemns the bringing of this s.ubject into party politics the resolution which he is going to support and for which he is going to vote makes it immediately a party question, because the resolution is brought to condemn the action of the gov-' ernment in not having established a fast line. I am with the hon. gentleman in his desire to keep this out of party politics, and I want to repeat that it is a fortunate thing that we did not establish a fast line before now, because now we do get it-and I think it is going to come perhaps sooner than some people expect-we will have the best and the fastest line, superior to anything that crosses from Europe to New York, and nothing else will satisfy us.

If we get this fast line must we not improve it every hour and keep it up to date ? If we had got it ten years ago we would have had to improve it every hour and keep it up to date. This will go on just the same. Changes will come and we will have to adopt them.

The subject under discussion-a fast line steamship service-is one that has engaged the attention of parliament for some years, and one which has been looked upon with much favour by many Canadians interested in having ourselves as Canadians keep pace with our neighbours to the south of us.
When we consider that Halifax is 400 miles nearer old England-the world-centre of trade -than New York and that the port of Halifax is second to none in America for approach and safety when in it, I can see no reason why we should lack in enterprise, why we should not be equal to the emergency, act upon our impulses, and have a line of steamers to compete with our neighbours. It is humiliating to find Canadians, when taking a trip to England, leaving Canada and going to New York, away from the objective point, in order to find a fast line boat to accomplish such a voyage, and the same returning, when we can so readily have a service of our own. I want to see the condition

of matters reversed, and we Canadians have a fast line of our own, with Halifax, so to speak, the New York of Canada, as well as the entrepot of trade, offering inducements for Americans to come to Halifax and embark for the old world, from that point, and vice versa, which we will find quite within our reach, if we set about it determined to have it.
If Halifax could only see herself as others see her, if she would free herself from that lethargy which has possessed her in the past, if she would think of the future which is hers, and bestir herself, with the determination to realize the duty she owes to herself and the country, with the great natural advantages within her grasp, she could be all she desires to be. She could be the chief depot of trade for Canada, and for enterprise and thrift a second New York.
But there is one thing that suggests itself to me, as a matter of vital importance, in connection with: the protection of life and property, and that is the course these fast line boats should be required to take for the safety of the lives of fishermen engaged in the fisheries on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. The ocean track for steamers at present plying between Great Britain and Halifax is across the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, which means devastation, swift and sure, to any vessels found at anchor in the track of any of these boats moving along at a fast rate of speed. When the horizon is clear, danger from these boats can be seen and averted by signals, fog trumpets or guns, but when the fog shuts down and the storm king rides with fury on the blast, preventing the sound of the fog trumpet or gun from being heard, or when the fog prevents the discernment of the lights of an approaching ship in the distance, the ship, with her speed unabated in order to accomplish a quick passage, ruthlessly presses forward when crossing the banks, regardless of the lives of the poor fishermen. Then it is that death, swift and sure to all vessels' crews in their track is occasioned.
But for this risk, the life of the fisherman is a comparatively pleasant one. The fishermen often in conversation express themselves as being regardless of danger, feeling when at sea on board their vessels, which are seaworthy, staunch and strong, such as those composing the fleet from my county, as safe as if they were on land, and to emphasize this expression of feeling, they can truthfully and with a happy, fight, good, loyal, hearty ring, sing the old familiar song : A life on the ocean wave,
A home on the rolling deep.
Or the more pathetic one, * Rocked in the Cradle of the Deep.' Or when the fisherman returns to his domesticated home, ' The Cottage by the Sea.'
On behalf of this class of hardy, brave fishermen, to whom much of the success of Nova Scotia depends, my county in particu-
Iar, I must ask if it is not possible to have the attention of other countries called to the many risks attending fishermen on the Grand Banks when pursuing their calling, and have an arrangement made with the United States and the old world, through their respective boards of trade, and they with their respective governments, with the object of having all lines of steamers traversing the north Atlantic between America and the old world, excepting those going north of Newfoundland, take a course along the southern edge of the Grand Banks, and south of Sable island, which would carry them free of all the fogs of the banks, and the risks of icebergs, and better still, avoid the risk of the destruction, as I have stated, of the lives and property of fishermen.
I would ask the government to consider this matter very carefully, so important to our fishermen, and endeavour to effect an arrangement on the lines I have suggested.

I am paired with the hon. the leader of the opposition, or otherwise I would have voted against the amendment.

I wish to call the attention of the Postmaster General to a matter which is of sufficient importance to the Canadian public to merit the attention of this House for a few moments. During the last few days hon.

members of this House will have noticed that the corridors have been flooded and covered up with an immense number of mail bags containing campaign literature.
I would not object to that, if it did not interfere with the ordinary postal service of the country, but I am informed on reliable authority that the distribution of this matter through the mails is seriously interfering with our postal service. The post office of the House and the post office in the city are glutted with this matter ; the railway postal cars are over-laden and, what is more -serious still, newspaper publishers in Montreal have been unable to obtain mail bags in which their papers are sent to the post office for distribution to subscribers, the supply of mail bags having been 'cornered.' This is a serious state of affairs, and I would ask the Postmaster General if any complaint has come to him from newspaper publishers, or from any other citizens ?*
Oh.

It occurs to me, Sir, that this is no laughing matter at all. Several days ago I sent some correspondence through the mail to my home at Regina, and I received word last evening that it had never been delivered. I am informed that this has been caused by the congestion in the mail service throughout Canada, as a result of the flooding of the mails with tons, and car-loads, and cargoes of campaign literature, franked through this House, and samples of which we have seen for some days piled up in the corridors and incommoding the members generally. If the privilege that is given to members of this House to frank mail matter is to be so flagrantly abused, it sterns to me that an amendment to the existing regulations has become imperative. It is rumoured also that one reason for the length of this session is to be found in the fact that the opposition have prolonged it purposely in order that they may have an opportunity of franking these car-loads of campaign literature during the session.
Oh.

This is not a laughing matter either, and the taxpayers of Canada will not consider it a laughing matter. One hon. gentleman on the other side of the House calculated that it costs no less than $28 a minute to keep the session of parliament going. When the taxpayers of Canada realize that it costs so much tio keep this House in session, week after week and month after month, simply to allow the opposition to frank their campaign literature, these taxpayers will not consider it a laughing matter. We have evidence, day after day, of the purpose of gentlemen opposite to uselessly keep the House in session. It is true that such -questions as the fast Atlantic service and provincial autonomy for

the North-west Territories are questions of real importance ; but is it not a fact that for the three months, from the first of May to the end of July, our friends on the other side were simply marking time by pretending to criticise the estimates. Ever since I was a boy I have heard the members of an opposition described as being the watchdogs of the treasury ; but surely never were there watch-dogs who could satisfy the appetite of contention propensities with such small bones as the members of this opposition were picking here for three months this summer. They took one whole night discussing, hour after hour, the matter of soft pork ; for hours on another occasion they devoted their whole time to discussing the price of two wheel-barrows, and on a third occasion they gave us their views for an entire evening on an alleged exorbitant charge of 25 cents in the cost of an axe. These may be matters of interest, but we have the Public Accounts Committee for the special purpose of, considering such questions, and surely it is not meet to keep an august body, such as this House, in session week after week and month after month, discussing such picayune things. I repeat that this is no laughing matter to me, and 1 believe that the people of the country will not consider it a laughing matter. My hon. friend (Mr. Marcil, Bonaven-ture) has acted very properly in drawing the attention of the Postmaster General to the subject. X understand that the system followed by the Postal Department is that, as a matter of courtesy, the newspaper offices are allowed a certain number of these bags, which are the property of the Crown. They are taken to the office of publication and there utilized for the ordinary circulation of the newspaper. It seems that a newspapers publisher in Montreal, who is engaged in the laudable work of printing and publishing these tons and car-loads of campaign literature, has taken illegitimate advantage of the courtesy which is extended to newspaper publishers, and through their connivance this literature is sent in the bags to the members of the opposition here for the purpose of being franked, and we see it stacked around the corridors, and glutting the i:>ost office here and glutting the post office in the city. This is done to the detriment of other newspaper publishers who are deprived of the use of these bags which they need in their ordinary business. I trust that the Postmaster General will do his duty in this matter, and if it becomes necessary, that he shall confiscate, these bags and their contents and allow each newspaper publisher to receive his fair proportion of them.

As a sample of the inconvenience to which the general public are put, I may state that the Winnipeg newspapers-the ' Free Press,' the ' Tribune ' and the ' Telegram '-which should have been here two or three days
ago, have not yet reached Ottawa. I made inquiry as to the cause of this, and I was informed that they had left Winnipeg all right, but they had failed to reach here on account of this undue over-crowding of the mail service of the country. The files have had to be put away without these copies of the Winnipeg papers, and members from the west find it a great inconvenience now, as it will be a great deprivation in the future when they have to consult these files. I trust that the Postmaster General will do something to remedy this.

Complaint has been made to the department that certain newspaper publishers are not able to get their proportionate supply of these bags, because of the great numbers of them which are otherwise in use. I may explain to the House that for the convenience of the newspaper publishers it is the practice to allow them to have in their possession a number of these mail bags so as to enable them to forward their newspapers to the post offices in a convenient form. In that way, newspaper publishers of Canada are convenienced in the transmission of their papers to their ordinary subscribers. It appears that one leading publisher in the city of Montreal has improperly used these bags and diverted them to a purpose for which they were never intended. He has done that to the inconvenience of his fellow-publishers, and to the detriment of the rights of the public in general. The department is to-day unable to supply other publishers with bags for the transaction of their legitimate business.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: How many bags has this Montreal publisher used in this way ?

Thousands, I should say. My attention was called to the matter to-day by my officers, and I am informed that the deputy minister has been endeavouring to obtain possession of some of these bags. The publishers of ' La Presse' of Montreal cannot be supplied with bags.
Are they sending out literature too ?

I do not know what they are doing. They are engaged in the publication of a public journal, and they have their rights as well as other' publishers. My hon. friends have asked for information, and I am giving it. This question has been brought to the attention of the department in the ordinary course of business. Yesterday the supply of bags available at Montreal was exhausted, and one publisher could not get a single bag because of the absorption of the supply by hundreds and thousands, I expect by the one publisher in question, who has diverted those bags from the'proper use for which they were entrusted to him to this illegiti-

mate and scandalous transaction. If the hon. gentlemen who control these hags would be good enough to remove their contents and let us have the bags, then the business of the post office could be carried on. But I am not prepared to go to thousands of dollars of expense to purchase additional bags-even the making of them would involve a considerable time-simply to enable a procedure of this kind to be carried out, It does seem to me that a very grave abuse has been made of the privileges of parliament in this procedure. I doubt if parliament ever intended that tons and tons and carloads and trainloads of printed matter should be printed in different places in this country and sent post free to the city of Ottawa, to a member of parliament, under the provisions of the Act which allows such matter to come free; and that this same privilege should be so abused in the method which is mow being adopted. To-day the postmaster of the city of Ottawa has made a complaint to the department that he is unable to carry on the legitimate work of his office owing to the congestion of the building by the accumulations of mail matter there-this literature, as it is called, which has been dumped there in carloads every day. Moreover, the difficulty cannot be removed by any addition to the staff at the Ottawa post office or at the House of Commons post office. The cars have not the capacity to carry away this stuff. The postal cars are of limited capacity, and we have been filling them to accommodate lion, gentlemen opposite.
Could not some of the private government cars be used ?
And yet in spite of every effort that is being made, the accumulation is gaining upon us, and the public service is being prejudiced.
Mountains of information.

Whatever may be in it, I do not know. I am told that hon. gentlemen themselves made a very excellent use of a large portion of this literature, having for some reason consigned it to the flames. I do not know whether the balance is intended to be so used; but perhaps it is about as good a use as it could be put to. On that I offer no opinion. Speaking from a party standpoint, I regret what has been destroyed, because the more freely it could be circulated the better it would be for the Liberal party, Speaking departmentally, which is the only way in which I speak now, I would say that hon. gentlemen opposite are as much concerned as the government in the proper management of the postal service, and I think it is inconsiderate on their part to deluge the service with this immense quantity of mail matter, which is treated as all other mail matter without any partiality. Every letter that goes through the post office

receives the same treatment, without priority; and this literature, which everybody knows is of no very great importance, is for the time being inconveniencing the officers in the carrying on of the legitimate work of the post office, which is, so directly concerned with the convenience of the public generally.

I infer from the remarks of the hon. Postmaster General that the opposition is sending out this literature. I know that my county is flooded with the speeches of the hon. Minister of Finance, and I would like to know what channel they come through.

I have not heard anything about the speeches of the Finance Minister. I am now alluding to these enormous accumulations that are seen in the corridors and passages of this building, that have blocked the business of the post offices and the railway mail service of Canada. I am speaking of that literature, be it from one side of the House or the other. But this accumulation arises from the particular class of literature to which I have alluded, which has been despatched in postal bags to the whip of the opposition, to be redistributed by him throughout Canada. I want these bags, as the property of the Crown, to be forthwith returned to the Post Office Department. Unless they are delivered there, I shall have to exercise the authority of a Minister of the Crown and take possession of them. I beg to say, in all seriousness, that we are to-day without mail bags for the proper convenience of the subscribers to the press of this country. We have sufficient of that class of property, but it is unfortunately at this moment out of the control of the government. Enormous numbers of these bags are under the control of an hon. member of this House, and I ask him here to return those bags forthwith-
Lay them on the Table ?
Or I will take steps to take possession of them by force of law. We do not desire in the slightest degree to interfere with the use of the franking privilege.
When does the hon. gentleman propose to take possession of them ?

1 am giving notice now. If I am asked to specify a time, I will do so. I will give the hon. gentleman to-day to deliver those bags to the proper officers, and if they are not delivered by Monday morning, I will take steps to take possession of them.
Don't get mad.

I am not at all. I propose to try to protect the crown in its own rights, and in doing that

to protect the citizens of the country in their legitimate rights. I maintain that the public of Canada are not called upon to submit to the inconvenience and the injury to which they are now subject because of this gross violation of the privileges of parliament. When a member of this House finds himself in possession of mail bags which are marked the property of the crown, the property of the Post Office Department, it is his duty at the earliest moment to return them to the government to whom they belong; and when they come to him illegitimately, as they did in this case, that duty is a much more pressing one on his part. It was a gross violation of the privilege granted to the publisher of that newspaper to divert these bags from the purpose for which they were entrusted to him; and it is my intention not to allow that same publisher any more to be entrusted with bags until guarantees are given that they will not be diverted from the use to which they ought properly to be put.

The hon. the Postmaster General has given us an exhibition which is hardly becoming his dignity and hardly worthy of the office he fills. He has spoken of that illegitimate' and scandalous use of bags.
Hear, hear.
Illegal.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is it illegal or improper to do what the law provides may be done ?
What does the law provide may be done ?

It provides that any matter may be sent free to any member of this House during the session of parliament, and any matter, franked by any member, shall go out free, whether it goes out in single papers or by the bag full.
Would the hon. gentleman contend that it is legal for a publisher, who had possession of these bags, to make use of them in the way he is doing ?
The law provides that publishers of newspapers shall have the right to send here mail matter, and by regulation of the department, for the sake of convenience, bags are furnished for that purpose.	_
They were not.
And he is not using them improperly or illegally.
He Is.

Mail matter going out of the post office franked by any member of this parliament, whether it goes out in single papers or by the dozen, or in mail bags,
is going out in accordance with the law and is neither illegal nor scandalous. The members of the opposition are exercising their undoubted right in sending the matter through this post office, when franked as the law provides. That is all they are doing. Reference is made to the fact that in the corridors large piles of these bags are found, may they not as well be found there as in the Public Works Department, or some of the other departments, where civil servants, who are paid by the country, are employed to address and mail them ? I am informed that such is the case.

There is not one iota of foundation for that statement. Not one bag nor one-lialf a bag lias been sent out from the Public Works Department nor has any employee of that department been engaged in any such work.
Does the hon. gentleman deny that there are not employees in some of the departments sending out these speeches ?

I cannot speak, any more than can the hon. gentleman, for other parts of the city. He mentioned the Public Works Department in particular, and I say here, in the presence of everybody, that not one bag nor one-half bag, nor any literature, has been mailed from that department, and no employee connected with that department lias been engaged on any such work.
I was credibly informed
Take it back.

I was creditably informed that such was the case, but of course I accept most unreservedly the denial of the hon. minister. I was told that in some of the departments this is being done, and the Department of Public Works was mentioned as one of them. However, whether they come from that department or not, we know for a fact that speeches of the leader of the government and the Minister of Finance and others were sent out by the thousands, franked by members of parliament. They are not sent through the post office in this building, and therefore are not to be found in the corridors, but they are sent out from elsewhere, and I think improperly, because they should go from this post office, if franked, which, I am told, they are. They should be sent from here, but they are not at present ; and the only difference is that in the one case you see the matter in these corridors and in the other you do not. I am told that while the Postmaster General says that these bags are being sent out by the thousand, there were only all told 140 bags in the corridors.

I do net know whether there are more than 140 bags

there at the one time, hut I am told that there are large quantities in store at Ottawa waiting until this great mass in the corridors is removed, and then they will be set in their places. They are coming up in wagon loads at all hours of the day. The accumulation may be only 140 at this moment, but I expect that thousands of them have been taken away.
There is not a member of this House who would believe for one moment that these bags reached the number of one thousand.
There are several thousands.

The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) should be the last man in the world to object to the distribution of knowledge, because I do not know of anybody who needs, it more. And hon. members should remember that the country requires information to-day more than anything else. Are these hon. gentlemen afraid to let their light shine before the world and their deeds be known ? It is because they dare not let what is taking place in this House be made known throughout the country, that they object to this so strenuously. The hon. gentleman has said that this thing has tended to lengthen the session a month. That is not the case. What has lengthened the session ? Why, the government business has not been down until quite lately. We have been in session over seven months and the government has not got its work all down yet. Only a few nights ago the last supplementary estimates came down and we were told that there are more coming down with regard to the Quebec bridge. When did the railway subsidies come down ? Only a few days ago. Supplementaries containing over $10,000,000 only came down the last two weeks, yet forsooth the opposition are to be held responsible for the length of the session. Surely the hon. gentleman could not expect the country to take any stock in such a statement. The hon. gentleman spoke of what the increased length of the session cost the country. It does not cost the country a dollar more. An amount is voted for the session and whether the session be long or short, it practically makes very little difference. It Is the poor members of parliament who have to suffer.
What about employees who are paid by the day 1
They are paid a very small sum.
Does that not increase the cost of the session ?
Is it true or not that the Postmaster General pays these men $25 a month at the post office for stamping and sending out that literature ?

There is no man in the service of the Post Office Department who is paid so small a sum as $25 per month.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Eecess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When you left the Chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, we were dealing with the question which was raised by the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) with regard to what he was pleased to call, and what the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) afterwards termed, a scandalous and illegitimate use of the Post Office Department. No more ill-advised words could be spoken by a minister of the Crown. As members of parliament, we are here to do the work of the country, and what we are doing is within our undoubted right. The law provides that mail matter shall be sent free from this House to any portion of the country, when it is franked by a member of parliament and put in the custody of the Post Office Department. That done, the department is bound to take care of it until it is either delivered to the party to whom it is addressed or returned to the party from whom it is sent. In view of this, the statement made by the Postmaster General as to what he would do or would not do seemed to me rather unbecoming. I am glad that the Postmaster General, who was absent when I began to speak, is now present. I hope he is in better humour than he seemed to be before six o'clock. It was said-I think, by Mark Twain-that if you fill an Englishman up with roast beef and porter you may even venture to approach him with a subscription list. I hope that now that the Postmaster General has had a good dinner he has come here in a less belligerent and more amiable mood than he seemed to be in before recess.
I am always amiable.

And I hope he has forgotten the threat he made that if, by Monday morning these bags are not away, he would do so and so. Any attempt on his part to carry out that threat might be attended with serious consequences. In the first place it might obstruct the corridors of the House -of Commons.

I am afraid it would.
Mr. SPROULE-because, as members of parliament we have certain rights. The government is bound to provide us with conveniences for doing the work of the people which we have been sent here to do. That was our stuff that is in those bags, and it has been duly franked and put in possession of the Post Office Department.

1423a
It is not franked yet.

Yes a good portion of it is franked and is there waiting for the Postmaster General's Department to take it away. But, because the kon. gentleman has not provided enough assistance in the office, it cannot he taken away. But it has been handed over to his department.
No, it has not.

It is there to be taken away. Well, if the hon. gentleman's threat is carried out, what would be the result V These corridors would be blocked. We have not enough room. We have not the luxurious apartments of the Postmaster General and his friends taking up practically one-third of the room of the House of Commons. We have a little 7x9 room for our accommodation. Lazarus like, we are trying to subsist on the crumbs that drop from the rich man's table. If the Postmaster General should endeavour to carry out his threat, I have no doubt there would be insistence. There is too much of the Anglo-Saxon domination in this part of the country to allow that threat to be carried out without some effort to prevent it. Every man who is a man stands up for his rights. It is said that even a worm will turn if you tread upon it. Perhaps the Postmaster General feels that he can turn to his friend the Minister of Militia, and get the militia turned out to support him. But let me remind him that that would involve heavy expense which the city would have to pay, and they would hold him to serious account for it. It would hardly increase his popularity. So, I think that after serious consideration he will hardly carry out that threat. At any rate, we hope he will not.
One of the hon. members on the other side said that we had destroyed a lot of literature. We did dstroy a lot of literature- we are free to admit it. And why did we destroy it ? Because, through some mistake, the figures were wrongly given, and to put those figures before the people would have been to mislead them. So, we destroyed that literature, every sheet of it. Would the Postmaster General desire that it should be sent out to mislead the people and give them a wrong impression. We thought it more honourable, more manly to destroy it.
Are there no mistatements in what is going out ?
We believe not.
The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) pointed out-

To the best of our knowledge and belief, the statements made in the literature now going out are correct. But we would not send out literature containing errors which we knew to be errors. Now,
I	say that, as members of parliament, we have a right to send out this literature. It is now the property of the parties to whom the different pieces are addressed. It is franked and addressed and in the possession of the Post Office Department, and the Post Office Department is bound to deliver it or return it to us. Why is not that literature sent away ? We are told, when we endeavour to get it away, that the Post Office Department has not a sufficient number of hands to do the work, and the Postmaster General will not allow them to engage more.
That is not true.
I believe it is absolutely true.

Then the hon. gentleman believes something that is absolutely untrue. The staff of the department is ample. The trouble is that the cars are not sufficient and the train accommodation is over-taxed. It would take train after train to carry the stuff. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been sending away carloads every day.
I am only telling the hon. gentleman what is told us.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) often rises and says that he is credibly informed so and so. Just before six o'clock he said that he was informed something about the Public Works Department which turned out to be absolutely untrue. Yet he said he was * credibly informed.' Now, he is ' credibly informed.' Will he give me the name of his informant ?

That is a handsome request on the part of the Postmaster General. I wonder that he is not ashamed to ask it. Would he want to penalize one of his own employees because of a statement made by him that there were not enough hands in the Post Office Department ?
Will! the hon. gentleman name his informant 7

I made a statement which I believed to be true, and where I am known I will match my reputation for veracity against that of the Postmaster General any day. I do not come here and make statements that I do not believe to be correct, and I deny the right of the Postmaster General to contradict me. I made the statement on the authority of the chief whip (Mr. Taylor) who sits beside me, made to me fifteen minutes before. So, was not I justified in repeating that statement ? I have a character to maintain, and I will not allow any man to call my veracity in question even though he be called the Postmaster General.
Oh, oh.

I am within my rights.
II	made a statement before six o'clock, that

I was gredibly informed that certain material was being sent through the mails from the Public Works Department. I have made inquiries since, and I find that the stuff is being sent out, but that I happened to be wrong about the department from which it was going. It is being sent out in large quantities, and I am told that it is being addressed by the civil servants who are paid by the country. On the other hand, we are paying for this work out of our own scanty means, and we are working night and day to send out this literature to the country. We are doing only what it is our right and our duty to do, and, instead of being abused, we ought to be commended for it. We are doing what is strictly within our legal right. But what did hon. gentlemen opposite do in this matter of abusing the franking privilege. Sir Richard Cartwright sent out, I was told, about a ton of matter. It was sent out between sessions. It was not in any sense an official document of this parliament, but a speech made on the public platform, printed here and sent out under the frank of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, sent out improperly, wrongfully, illegally. On the other hand, we are doing what the law gives us a perfect right to do, and no more. It is true we were mislead by the government. We began to send this literature out because we were mislead into believing that an election was coming on.
Now we have it.

It is the right of the opposition to try to enlighten the people of the country. Are hon. gentlemen opposite afraid that the people will be too much enlightened, that the record of the government will be placed too plainly before the people. When we began to send out this literature the government got scared and backed out, and now we are told they are not going to the country. It is said that we liavte lengthened1 the session, adding greatly to the cost. Is that the ease ? What does the hon. gentleman know about it who made that statement ? Is it not the fact that we are here practically by the job -we get $1,500 for the session, whether that session last thirty days, or nine months, or a year. We get no more and no less ; it entails no additional charge on the country. The Speaker of the House gets' the same salary whether the session is two months or twelve months; so do the Clerk and the Assistant Clerk and the other officials. Who gets what additional cost is imposed on the country by the increased length of the session ? A few of these little pages, the messengers and the sessional clerks and writers, who are paid by tbe day, these poor people who are dependent upon their daily labour for their subsistence, and the government begrudges them even the few days of additional work they get by reason of the increased length of the session. The page hoys get $1.50 a day, and the government Mr. SPROULE.
would rather cut them off from that ; the same thing applies to the messengers and the sessional writers. The allegation of increased cost is entirely incorrect and misleading. I said before and I say again that we should be rather commended for our industry. We are engaged in an onerous, arduous, honest and faithful work ; we are distributing the records of parliament, which should be always acceptable, and no men should be more pleased to find them distributed to the electors of the country, who must after a while give their verdict, than the hon. gentlemen opposite. Is that an improper or a wrong work or one for which the opposition should be abused ? I say it is not, and I only ask that the government 8110111(1 give us as an opposition fair-play. We are only exercising the rights to which we are entitled by virtue of our position as representatives of the people. We are doing no injustice to the government in exercising these rights. If they do not provide accommodation for us to do our work in any other place than the corridors of this building, we must do it in the corridors, and if the mail bags of the country will not hold these papers we will have to empty them In the corridors, because they must be handled by the Post Office Department whether the government likes it or not; that belongs to the people. It is unfair to blame the opposition for doing no more than what they are sent to do by the country and the stigma is cast on the electors rather than on the representatives. I can tell the Postmaster General and his colleagues that when the time comes the people will resent that stigma, and that they will have to settle with the people and uqt with us for the tirade of abuse they have heaped on us because we have endeavoured to enlighten the people on matters on which it is our duty to enlighten them.

I do not think I can be charged with taking up much of the time of this House. As a representative of the west, a man who lives 3,000 miles from here, I protest at the way in which the business of the House is being kept back by people who certainly should know better. One hon. gentleman has sat in this House for five and twenty years; during this session I have sat in the House every day except three, and I have never heard any little question of business discussed that the hon. gentleman did not enlarge upon it. There is not a member in this House who took up as much time as the hon. gentleman.
If the hon. gentleman talks only about what be knows, it is no wonder he does not talk much.

I do not think it is right or fair that we who live a long distance from here and have other things to look after should be kept here to hear the empty vapourings of people who want

to air their views in which no one is interested. As far as I am concerned, I am prepared to sit here as long as any good is being done, but I cannot see how any good is being done in a case of this kind. A statement was made a few minutes before six o'clock that there _are 140 bags in the corridor. To my personal knowledge there are 735 bags around this House, all full of this literature. I do not object to this literature, but I do say that it is an abuse of the franking system. Perhaps, as a young member, I should not say that kind of thing, but I do not think the law was intended to cover a case of this kind, whether the literature is sent out either by the government or by the opposition. These bags average 90 pounds each, and if the postage on their contents was paid by the men who should pay for it out of their own pockets, It would cost $2,940 to pay for what is now being franked. I am told that for the last 40 days an average of 150 bags a day, filled with this literature, have gone out. That is some 6,000 bags, and taking five bushels to the bag, we have '30,000 bushels, and with 1,000 bushels to the carload we have 30 carloads of literature which have been sent out from here at the expense of the people of this country. I have heard hon. gentlemen denounce in unmeasured terms the small salaries paid to railway clerks and employees. I quite agree that the railway clerks should be well paid, for I know many railway clerks who have to go into a car piled to the ceiling with this literature; they are expected to do work in that car and are paid' a small salary fordoing it. Members should pay for the literature which they send out; if I have literature to send out, I will pay for it myself, and every man should do the same thing. The franking privilege is meant to extend only to the ordinary courtesy of sending parliamentary papers to constituents.
We have heard a good deal about the mail bags, and now we have had a lesson from what I might call one of the wind-bags.
Order.

I take it back, but I must say that when the hon. gentleman or any other new member of this House undertakes to belittle the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) he undertakes something that neither he nor any other man can do in this country. That hon. gentleman had a reputation in this House long before the hon. gentleman who has just spoken was ever heard of, and he will have a reputation after many who are now criticising 'him will have passed out of the public eye. Returning to the question, I understand that under the Act we have a right to send any parcel up to four pounds and the Post Office Department is bound to accept it and take care of it. We have not in any way exceeded the rights which we
possess. If any one wishes to dispute what I am about to say, let it be submitted to the Committtee on Privileges and Elections or any other committee and see if we cannot prove that for every day almost of this session, or at least since literature commenced to be sent out, the Liberals have sent out from 25 to 50 bags. All of this has been stamped, and in every way the Liberals have been taking advantage of their rights; yet now, when our literature is being held back because we are not able to get it out on account of their literature, the lion. Postmaster General, forsooth, is going to take the bags and distribute them. We will wait until we see him. The Liberals have sent out a much larger quantity of literature than have the Conservatives. 250,000 copies of the Premier's speech on the transcontinental railway have been sent broadcast through this country, bearing the franks of hon. gentlemen opposite. We are sending out the speeches of our deader and of the hon. gentleman whom our friends opposite admired and still admire, the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and canals, so that the people of the country may have that side of the question also. Then, in addition to the speeches that are being sent out from Ottawa, I understand that the Montreal ' Herald ' is having some hundreds of thousands of the speeches of the hon. gentlemen distributed amongst other Liberal papers through the country and inclosed as a supplement, thereby taking advantage of the mails in order to distribute these speeches among the people.
Do we hear the bon. Postmaster General arising and finding fault with that ? No, not at all. These are things to be investigated, and while they are emptying the bags we will be there to see. Hon. gentlemen talk about a lengthy session, forsooth. We have had a session the like of which has never been known in the history of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite have voted away more millions than has ever been voted away in any session in days gone by. It is hard to believe that it would be possible for men in their sound senses to think of voting away $120,000,000 for a railway. Then we have had a railway Bill that took up two months of the session, followed by a Redistribution Bill, some of these important measures being brought down three months after ^he House met. The House was called together months after it should have assembled. It was not called together until March 12 thus subjecting to inconvenience every man coming from the outlying districts of this country. If the government did not know that, they should have known it. They have taken advantage of the members of this House in bringing them here at the time they did, yet we 'hear hon. gentlemen getting up and making the statements that we have listened to to-day. The Conservative party will be prepared to justify before the public

-every action they have taken. Hon. gentlemen opposite may bring on the election to-morrow or the next day or the week after, and we will be prepared to go on any platform and before any public audience in this country and discuss every question, and we will also be round when they are emptying the mail bags.

I am not aware that I have said to any hon. gentleman that he was not at liberty to exercise the franking privilege. Parliament leaves it to each hon. gentleman to exercise the franking privilege in accordance with the true spirit of the Act. That is not the real subject under discussion. The question came up as to the shortage of mail bags for the press, and I stated that the reason of the shortage was that the courtesy of the department had been disregarded by a leading paper, which had received a certain quantity of bags for the proper use of the publisher, but which bad been improperly used. I say that again. I say that we have allowed this newspaper, bags for the purpose of inclosing their own papers to be sent to the post office for transmission amongst their subscribers, and that the publisher has abused that privilege, because, instead of using the bags for that purpose, be has diverted them to this other purpose, withdrawn them from circulation and thus interfered with the right of co-publishers, making it impossible for the department to supply bags to other publishers of papers for the purpose of distributing their papers. The use of bags for the purpose to which Mr. BOYD.
these have been put is contrary to the purpose for which they were loaned. These bags belong to the department, and unless they are returned the department will take steps to repossess itself of them.
We have heard the explanation of the hon. gentleman. This little piece of theatricals has all been over a few mail bags.
Thousands of them.
What kind of facilities is the hon. gentleman giving this country, when he has only a few mail bags ?
The best it ever had ; far better than the Tories gave it.
He is telling us that they have a few mail bags.
Thousands.
He says a thousand.
I say thousands.

I venture to say that the hon. gentleman is again wide of the mark. Even if it is 2,000, it does not affect the question. 1 ask the hon. gentleman if he, as Postmaster General, and his department are not bound to furnish all the facilities necessary to carry the mail matter from any newspaper office in this country that may be legitimate mail matter ?
No ; there is nothing whatever in the law compelling us to take mail matter from the publishers. We carry it from the post office when it is delivered there.

That is what the hon. gentleman is doing now. The hon. gentleman knows very well that the franking privilege does not belong to the members of this House alone. During the session of parliament it belongs to every elector in Canada. He may send his mail matter within the limits prescribed by the regulations of the department to this House. What has been done by this publisher ? He has complied literally with the law. He has not violated a single particle of the law, and he has done this for the convenience of the Post Office Department. Is the hon. gentleman going to confess that he has run out of a few mail bags ?
Thousands.
The hon. gentleman has run out of thousands ?
No, he has not.

The country will know that the hon. gentleman's department is

well equipped. If he is not prepared to cope with the Montreal ' Herald ' and to carry the speeches of the right hon. First Minister and of the hon. Minister of Finance-all properly within the law, and no person is complaining of it-because he has a number of mail bags distributed over the country, the people of the country will understand how well equipped the hon. gentleman's department is. If these few mail bags are not returned to him, he says there will be a fuss over it.
Call in the police.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) says call in the police. I think the police might very well be called in to take charge of the hon. Postmaster General. I tell the hon. gentleman he has no more right to empty those mail bags than any other person has, and I do not think the hon. gentleman will undertake to empty them, notwithstanding his threat. The hon. gentleman is greatly disturbed over a few mail bags. Does "the hon. gentleman know that two or three years ago in the Department of Agriculture the stamp of the hon. Minister of Agriculture- was used improperly and illegally for the purpose of sending out literature ? Does the hon. gentleman know that when some one stated that between
2,000	and 3,000 copies of the speech the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) had delivered at Massey Hall had been sent out, that the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce stated himself that it was more nearly 10,000 copies ? Yet this was done right under the eye of the Postmaster General, and with his sanction and connivance the law was violated.
That is wholly without foundation.
The hon. gentleman had better not make that statement, or I will take occasion before this House adjourns to produce the frank of the hon. minister of whom I have mentioned.
The hon. gentleman said, that with my knowledge and contrivance-my knowledge and connivance
And contrivance too.

The hon. gentleman said that with my knowledge and connivance the Minister of Trade and Commerce had transmitted large numbers of copies of his speech at Massey Hall through the post office. I do not know what the Minister of Trade and Commerce may have done; he will answer for himself; but I do know that no minister has ever, with my knowledge or connivance violated the franking privilege.

I am glad that the Postmaster General made that qualification, and
has found a means of escape. I will take his word for it, as I am bound to do; but I want to ask if the Postmaster General was not a little less vigilant in that case than in this. Did those who are now complaining call his attention to that matter ?
Not a bit of it ?

Not a bit of it. Will the Postmaster General be a little fair now. What is there wrong in this ? Who has violated any law; who has violated even good taste, if it be a matter of taste ? I want to tell the Postmaster General that it is not costing the country a dollar.

Yes, it
is.

The taxpayers are not paying one cent extra for this. The Postmaster General has not increased his staff in the post office here; there has not been an additional employee brought into the service, and therefore it has cost the people nothing. The Postmaster General knows perfectly well that a rush of matter like this passing through the mails temporarily, costs the country nothing. Therefore it costs the people of Canada not one farthing for the distribution of that literature. Where is the complaint then ? Is the Postmaster General or the leader of the House going to Intercept that knowledge which is going to the country ?
Knowledge ?

Yes; knowledge on a great question is being sent out broadcast, and this is the first time in the history of Canada that any one has been told they are sending out worthless literature, when they are sending out the literature of which these gentlemen opposite themselves are guilty. The hon. gentleman cannot silence public opinion or public sentiment. Neither can he intervene, and shake out this mail matter from the mail bags into the corridors. If he does, his employees will have to pick it up again and send it to the people. The House has never witnessed such a scene as we have witnessed this afternoon. I hope the Postmaster General will profit by the exhibition he made here.
Don't have any such hope.
He gave us an exhibition of bad taste and bad temper.
It was an abuse of the privileges of the House.

My hon. friend says it is an abuse of the privileges of the House, and I say it is not becoming to the dignity of a minister, who only a few nights ago told us how well his department was managed, to now come down and announce that Canada has run short of mail bags, and that he

cannot possibly furnish mail bags to a great newspaper in this country. Let me tell him that it is the duty of a Postmaster General, whether he be Liberal or Conservative, to meet the demands for distributing such literature, whether he may agree with it or not. If the Postmaster General is short of mail bags lne bad better get more. An apology is due from him at this moment; an apology is due from him, that with all the resources at bis disposal, he is not able to meet the requirements of the mail service of the country, and I trust that be and his friends will not again precipitate such a scene in a hurry.
The members on this side of the House were watching the countenance of the Postmaster General for an hour or two before be broke loose. We could not understande what was the m utter with him.
He was incubating.

Possibly he was. The whole House was admiring the genial countenance of the Prime Minister, but the Postmaster General looked dumb; there was something weighing him down, and at last we discovered what it was. He told us in his speech, that we were using thousands of mail bags, that it was scandalous, that it was an abuse of the privileges of the House, and then he stated that it would take a special train to carry these circulars up and down the country. Let me tell the Postmaster General, that these circulars were put into those mail bags for the convenience of his officers, and in doing so we were conferring a favour on this country, and doing work which his officials should have done. Not only was that done in the office of publication, but they were mailed as they had a perfect right to be mailed, to a member of this House, and that member was quite within his rights when he remailed them. He could have dumped them into the post office.
He could not get them in.

Yes, he could have piled these mountains of information up in the post office, and the Postmaster General dare not attempt to stop him. It was to relieve the hard worked and poorly paid post office officials of this country, that the Liberal-Conservative party went to the trouble of putting this mail matter into sacks. But the Postmaster General finds that this scheme to supplant the Prime Minister will not work. He finds that there is not going to be an election, in order that lie may have a possible opportunity of becoming Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada. We have noticed it in him on the street; we have noticed it in him in the * House, and we noticed it especially this' afternoon. He has shown dissatisfaction l

with things around him, and it is easy for us to conjecture what the cause of it all is. Now, he seeks to make a little cheap popularity in the country by attacking the Conservative party, and stating that his mail cars are overcrowded. If he is run out of mail cars, why does he not turn out two or three of the minister's private cars, and use them as mail cars ? If be has no postal cars why doesn't he take the government private cars and put his officers in them to distribute this mail, and enlighten the people of the Dominion ?
Sifton's car is not doing anything now.
Oh, yes it is.

The Postmaster General complains of these mail bags being seen in the corridor. I want to tell him that the Liberal-Conservative party does not go at night to a back street office in the town, and take the Postmaster General's frank, or the frank of his deputy, and ship circulars without their going through the regular post office here. What the Liberal-Conservative party does is done in the broad light of day; right in the House of Commons and the people of the Dominion of Canada can see what is going on, and we are not ashamed of what we are doing. The Postmaster General says that he has no mail bags ? Where have they gone ?
Several hundred of them are here now ?
You got down from the thousands.
Not half enough.

Well, here are some more : 230 bags at $1.05 ; 150 bags at $1. That is more than we have in the corridors now. Then I find:	cotton duck
pouches ; 140 at 30 cents, 477 at 30 cents, 114 at 25 cents. Cotton duck bags fitted with swivel, 18 at 35 cents ; cutting down jute sacks, 04 at 25 cents ; drag sacks, 6 at 95 cents ; 7,500 at 80 cents. Where have they all gone ? 4 at 85 cents ; 1 at 80 cents; 190 at 45 cents. Red striped linen bags : 48 at $1.65. 150 at $1.30, 24 at $1.25, 150 at $1.25, 150 at $1.15. 100 at $1.10. These are all from the Auditor General's Report for 1902, page S-11. If I had the report for
OCTjOBEB 17, 1903
this year, I am sure I could pile up a mountain of them. Then, here are yellow hags.
X suppose these are for the twelfth of July.
I wonder if the grand master saw any of them his way.
I must thank him very kindly.
That shows how considerate I was. Are there any green ones ?

I suppose the Postmaster General handles all kinds ; it does not make any difference what colour they are. Here are 150 at 40 cents, 100 at 25 cents, 24 at $1.16. Then I find an item : C. Warner, Ottawa, repairing cotton duck bags, 338 at 42 cents ; fitting with bars and ring, 452 at 5 cents ; repairing jute newspaper sacks, 801 at 41 cents ; fitting with cords, cases and ferrules, 481 at 0 cents. These must be some of the old patched bags which he is giving the Tory party. Then, here is a firm called' William Willis & Son, Aurora. It strikes me that Aurora is a little north of Toronto.
In North York, a fine place.

In North York, which the Hon. Postmaster General represents. I find these items for William. Willis & Son, Aurora : brown duck satchels, 25 at $1.80, 200 at $1.80, cotton duck folders, 73 at 45 cents, repairing mail bags, 6,732 at 25 cents, seamless cotton bags, 300 at 38 cents, 100 at 35 cents, 50 at 33 cents. I see also this item : T. H. Winter, Aurora, extra trips with mail bags between railway station and post office, 242 trips, which this gentleman made to the railway station carrying these mail bags to be' sent all over the country, and he charges 25 cents a trip. And yet the Postmaster General has the hardihood to stand up here and say that he is short of mail bags. I was surprised today to see the hon. member for Bon a venture (Mr. Marcil) get up when the Postmaster General turned his head around as if he had touched a button. You talk about the independence of parliament. Where was the independent spirit of that hon. gentleman when he would let any minister touch a button as a signal for him to get up and make an attack on the people, as he did today ? And where was the independence of the wild and woolly west, when the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) arose when the Postmaster General touched the button to say that a letter had been delayed. We all knew that the Postmaster General was possessed of a tyrannical spirit when he broke loose, but I hardly thought he could go the length he has done to day. I tell him that the hon. gentleman who put this matter in the mail bags did a service to the Post Office Department, and if he dares to take these mail bags, he and his 446
officials will have their work cut out for them in a different manner from what he expects. He may exercise his right to seize these mail bags; he may be within his authority if he does so.
No, no. '

Whether he is within his authority or not, he will not dare to do it. The hon. gentleman has made such an exhibition of himself to-day that it will take a lot of smiling and cajoling to put him in the estimation of this House and the country where he stood before.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
