House of Commons-further amount required for sessional clerks, $2,330.

This item is required on account of the length of the session. It provides for the payment of the sessional clerks to the 20th of this month. These estimates were prepared some time ago, when it was expected that this session would be over by that date.

Has any consideration been given to the representations that have been made to Mr. Speaker respecting increased remuneration for some of these men ? Are they being paid at the same rate, or is any increase being given to them ?
No. The sessional clerks are divided into three classes : one class at $3 a day, another at $3.50, and those who know shorthand and typewriting, at $4.
How does the number compare with the number formerly employed ?
It is just the same-25.
Is there any provision in this item for any extra pay for messengers and the officials about the doors ? Are they to receive any additional remuneration besides their per diem allowance ?
The longer the session, the better for them, because they are paid by the day and will receive more money.

Might I ask your consideration, Mr. Speaker, to the suggestion I dropped the other evening, to the effect that the members of the press gallery should be placed on the list of sessional clerks. Of course there are a few of the reporting staff who obtain more or less extra remuneration by reporting for the committees, but that is arduous work, and I am satisfied that they are entitled to all they earn in that way and that the country would endorse the action of Mr. Speaker, and the House in placing these gentlemen on the sessional staff. They do a great deal of work for the members and in this way save the increase of the sessional staff.
I have not had time to consider the matter very fully, hut I find on inquiry from the officers of the House that no such remuneration [DOT]was ever given in the past.
Would it not be a very good precedent to lay down ?
It is a very important question and 1 would not like to offer an opinion just now. We would be paying persons who are not at all under the control of the House.
They would be then.

I presume that the members of the press gallery would prefer to be absolutely free as they are to-day.
Debates-amanuenses. $560.
What is that for ?
The amanuenses are the young men who do the type writing for the reporters of the debates.
Are the debates not reported under contract ?

No, the debates reporters are officers of the House. The contract system was given up some twenty years ago.
Sessional messengers, $2,500.
How many have we ?
Forty-nine.
Are they paid by the day ?	.

Yes.
Ottawa public buildings-further amount required for Victoria Memorial Museum and other buildings, $100,000.

I am asking a general vote in view of the fact that last session in the main estimates there were some votes for two or three public buildings at Ottawa. I have not had a satisfactory plan made out yet; hut if we had this vote, we might during recess be able to make more satisfactory arrangements for the acquisition of sites.
The intention is to go on with the work ?
Yes.	'
Has the boil, minister any idea where it is to be located ?
No definite arrangement has been made. If I were to express myself favourable to one site as against another, it would be very difficult for me to obtain satisfactory prices.

I do not know whether it was this building which was meant, but I understood from the Finance Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
Minister that it was impossible to locate it on government property, but there was some adjoining property which could he had. He did not wish to say where it was because the price might be raised.

That is one of the matters under consideration. I shall have a further survey made to see whether or not the architect was mistaken. I am now having a survey of the property made. We may have to buy the adjoining property.

This system of voting the money without knowing the site is not the one which is followed in England. In this country the ministers contend that if it be known they intend purchasing property in any particular locality, they will have to pay two or three times as much for it; but, after all we are entitled to know where the site is before voting the money, and the government have always the power to expropriate and have a fair valuation made. It seems very odd to vote large sums without knowing where the money is to be expended.

I hope that this vote will meet with the approval of both sides. There is hardly a member of this House who has not, either by word or act, expressed his opinou that it is necessary we should have additional accommodation for our public buildings. I think that the hon. minister of Public Works is perfectly justified in asking for this amount in the way he has done. To have asked for a more definite vote would jeopardize whatever chance he may have for the purchase of a site at a reasonable price. There are two or three different sites in the city, which the owners would be very willing to sell, and for my part I would be perfectly satisfied to leave the matter in the hand of the minister, being convinced that he has the interests of the government and the department at heart and will choose the site best suited for the building. I hope that the vote will pass without further opposition.
Is this for the geological building ?
Yes.

I may congratulate the minister. It is pretty nearly time Canada bad a better Geological Museum and building generally. If he will proceed immediately with the purchase of the site and next year, if he should happen to be in office, go on with the immediate construction of the building, the House and the country will heartily endorse his action.
What progress is being made for the establishment of a mint?

The plans are being prepared and the question now is to obtain a site.

Public works-chargeable to income-public "buildings, Quebec, Que., hospital for treatment Of immigrants suffering from trachoma and kindred diseases, $12,000.

Representations were made some time ago that this building was necessary. On further consideration the matter was allowed to stand. Again the request was renewed, and it has been urged as a matter of great public interest. It has been reported that some of the immigrants are troubled with this disease, and there is danger that it will spread throughout the country.

Does not the hon. minister think it would be preferable to ship these immigrants back to their own country ? It seems to me a very singular thing that we should be obliged to establish a hospital for immigrants coming into the country, to cure them of this disease. It is a most unheard of proposition, to my mind a most scandalous proposition. I am surprised that the Minister of Public Works should bring in an estimate of this sort.
We are pretty well accustomed now to my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) using very extravagant language.
I am afraid I learned it from the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

The hon. gentleman is learning pretty fast apparently, for a new member. I have no doubt my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and others will understand the need for this building better than I do. It is for the purpose of ascertaining whether these immigrants have this disease. I understand from the medical officer that there is no way known to medical science to learn whether this disease is present without a careful examination. Some have been passed as free from this disease and have entered the country when they could not be sent back, though they actually had trachoma, and their being at large endangered the health of others.
It says that the building is for the treatment of these immigrants, not for examination.
If my hon. friend knows all about it he can hardly need my explanation.
They are there on probation?

Yes, and it may be-though I did not I confess, ask as to that point-that, in case they have the disease to some slight extent, they may be treated and cured. But the explanation given to me by the officers was that the object was to make a test of these immigrants.
446}
How do the American officials find out whether immigrants have this disease or not ?
Under the same system, I am informed; but I have no personal knowledge.
I understand that the American official at that port examines immigrants and excludes those suffering from disease.
They have a house of their own in Quebec.

If the explanation of the Minister of Public Works is correct, he is unfortunate in the choice of words in this estimate. It does not say a word about examining the immigrants to see if they are suffering from this disease, but it says ' hospital for treatment of immigrants suffering from trachoma and kindred diseases.'

I suppose the officials of the department are responsible for the wording, and it may not convey just the idea that the officials of the immigration branch of the Interior Department conveyed to me. I have not made the detailed inquiries, that, perhaps, I should have made, but I am sure they represented to me that the first and great object was to ascertain whether the immigrants have the disease or not.

As I belong to Quebec, and am more familiar than is my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) with the circumstances, I may give some explanation. This building has been made necessary in consequence of a state of facts which we discovered last year. It was found by the medical experts that we had in Quebec some of these immigrants coming from some part of Europe, who, though suffering from this disease had escaped detection at Grosse Isle. At Quebec they were suspected of suffering from trachoma and were detained at St. Rochs, where there is quite a congested population. At one time we had the house visited and found twelve patients. There was great danger of this disease contaminating the neighbourhood. It was too important a matter to be neglected, and we thought it would be better to have a house properly fitted, so that these sick people could be isolated, and the community protected from infection.

I understood the minister to say that it was the intention to put up a building so that these people might be separated from the others until they can be sent back. This is a contagious disease, there is no doubt; and, while some cases are curable, the great majority are not curable. I frankly confess that I think the course proposed is the proper one to take. These people cannot be isolated too soon,

because you intensify the evil by allowing the disease to spread.
Quebec military buildings-new iron foundry (revote). $4,800.
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. This amount was voted, but lapsed at the end of the fiscal year, the accounts not being in and ready for payment. I am asking for this revote so that the accounts may be paid. The same applies to the next item, which is for the new artillery workshop, $3,000.
Are these buildings completed 1

I think there is some more work to do in fitting them up.
Public buildings. Nova Scotia-Springhill public building, repairs, $7,000.
This is necessary on account of the unfortunate accident by which the man who was responsible for it and one of his comrades were killed. The building was damaged and the heating apparatus wrecked.
What was the cause of the accident ?

The man who was in charge was killed. The expert sent down to investigate reported that though everything was blown up, he found that two large valves which should have been opened were left closed, and the steam being unable to escape, had caused an explosion.
Public buildings, generally-immigrant buildings, $12,000.

This has been applied for by the Department of the Interior, and it is said that the need of these buildings is urgent. One of them was so urgent that we have undertaken to go on with the work. This is to be provided where the Barr colony is settled. A number of immigrants have come in late and have not provided themselves with housing for the winter. It is proposed to put up a temporary building to shelter them.

The utmost care should be taken and no expenditure spared to prevent any mishap occurring to these people this winter, because if there should be any mishap to them, no matter how improvident 'they may be, there would be' a stream of misrepresentation against Canada in the spring.

I quite recognize this, but the departments in these matters always want things done in a hurry and want a great deal of money, so that some one has to keep the brakes on. I have kept the vote as small as possible, but I recognize the truth of what the hon.

gentleman has said that even if there is some waste of money it would not do to have these people suffer.
Ville Marie wharf-Lake Temiscamingue, repairs, renewals, &c., $2,500.

The government have a small wharf at this place. There is quite a large settlement there, and the amount of trade growing up in that district is simply wonderful. I did not believe it myself until a deputation came down here and explained it to me. This is being done in order to enlarge the wharf so as to accommodate this growing trade.
Windsor harbour-sheer dams, training dykes and deepening River Avon (revote of lapsed amount), $700.
Are these all the votes that are to be taken for public works in Nova Scotia ?
All that I know of.

I have received a letter to-day asking for a permanent light at Bass river. The hon. Minister of Finance will know that there is at this point an important manufacturing concern headed by Messrs. Fulton. They are 15 or 20 miles from the railway, yet with the assistance of the summer shipping in the Bay of Fundy and by hauling to the station in winter, they are conducting a successful business in the manufacture of furniture, which is sent all over New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Although they have encountered many difficulties, such as fire, difficulties that would have discouraged most people, they have persevered and are doing a good deal of shipping on the Bay of Fundy. You built a wharf there a year or two ago, but Mr. Edward Fulton, who is a leading man in our county-unfortunately he is a Liberal, but in every other way he is a most distinguished man-writes me and complains that it is very difficult for the steamers to get into the wharf and that he has, in fact, to hold a lantern on the wharf in order to enable them to make it. They have to load the steamer whenever it can get in with the tide. Mr. Fulton thinks that $300 or $400 would be sufficient to put a permanent light there, which would enable the steamer to get in with less difficulty.
Does the hon. gentleman say that this Liberal wants to hold a light up to them ?

I do not wish to introduce any politics in the matter; Mr. Fulton is a very capable man, notwithstanding his politics, and a very good man. I would ask the hon. Minister of Public Works to see that in some way this accommodation is furnished.

Of course, it is too late to put anything in these

estimates. I know Mr. Fulton, the gentleman to whom my bon. friend (Mr. Gour-ley) has referred, and 1 know that his industry is an important one, but whether or not this light should be provided by the department is a matter which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will have to ascertain.
What good is your harbour if the steamer cannot get into it on the tides? It cannot get in at regular hours.
I think they need some light in Colchester county.
It takes such a trifle to provide a light of this kind that the government could take out a sufficient amount from the vote for lighthouses without having a special vote. .
The Minister of Finance has given a good reason; they want light in Colchester county; that is enough.

My hon. friend is right. I shall have to have a report made, and I will be glad to have this during the next week. There is a general vote out of which this light can be erected.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- steam service between Petit de Grat and the Intercolonial Railway terminus at Mulgrave, S3,000.
Explain this please.

This is an item for the purpose of establishing a service which will be a very important feeder to the Intercolonial Railway. It is to develop the fishing business of the eastern part of Nova Scotia, which has already been the subject of discussion on one or two occasions in this House. It is to develop the business of sending fresh fish from the eastern portion of Nova Scotia to the upper provinces and even to the western states. It is an important and growing business and It has given considerable traffic to the Intercolonial Railway already. This is for an extension of the steamship service in connection with this business. I have no doubt this will give a large amount of extra business to the Intercolonial Railway.
What steamer is going to be on this route ?
I do not know as that point has not been decided yet.
Surely we must have some finality as to subsidies. If we are going to subsidize steamers to carry trade to the Intercolonial, I think it is carrying the principle of subsidies to an absurd length.

I am sure there is no subsidy that we have voted for generations which is better entitled to consideration than this one. We have had discussions in this House as to the importance of developing this fresh fish industry and perhaps we could take no step which would more directly aid that industry than by making connections between the central fishing communities and the railway terminus at Mulgrave. There is a large fishing industry at Cape Canso, which has given a great deal of business to the Intercolonial Railway. This is to bring a similar traffic from Cape Breton and I feel quite sure that there is no money that we will spend that is more likely to develop business than this subsidy.
Where is Petit de Grat ?
It is in Richmond county, on the island Madame.
How large a place is it ?

It is a \ scattered fishing district. It is a community that has given a great deal of attention to the fresh fish business. The fresh fish business requires a very special organization. Where you have the ordinary fishing business, where the people cure their own fish that can be done in a small way, but if you establish a fresh fish business it needs a considerable amount of capital and organization. This subsidy is for the purpose of aiding a steamer to be put on the route for the purpose of gathering the fish and shipping it.

There are two steamers now plying in that vicinity. One of them runs from Canso to Arichat and the other one through the St. Lennox passage to St. Peters. I imagine one of them must pass Petit de Grat. I cannot at the moment recollect where Petit de Grat is. I think, though, that the steamer running through the St. Lennox passage must pass near to it.
This is on the other side of the island.
The Canso boat calls at Arichat.
The Canso boat is so fully occupied that she cannot perform this service.

This business began seven or eight years ago, and the first year there was received by the Intercolonial Railway from the business furnished by the industry at Canso, between $4,000 and $5,000. During last year the Intercolonial Railway received $27,000 from this business, and from one firm in Canso. There are other firms, and we expect that before long the Intercolonial Railway will have from [DOT] $75,000 to $100,000 of revenue from the transportation of fish from the Atlantic coast.
How much will come from Petit de Grat ?
It is more than probable that within five years a far larger revenue will be derived from that place than is derived from the Canso business at the present time.

This is a very good thing and I heartily concur in it. I believe that the only way you can gather fish for shipment to the western market is by steamer. I am going to ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) to go farther than he has gone. The same business is being developed in St. Mary's bay ports and in the Bay of Fundy. Fresh fish is being collected and taken to St. John for shipment over the Intercolonial Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway to Montreal. We have a boat there now which has managed to keep going as well as it can but it has not been working to advantage. It is, however, an immense accommodation to the fishermen, and while I would not ask the hon. minister for anything this session, I am in hopes that this experiment will prove so successful that next session he will be able to give a subsidy for a small boat to run from St. Mary's bay ports and the Bay of Fundy to St. John.
Will anybody put on a special steamer for this purpose ?
This vote is taken in the hope of inducing some parties to put on an extra boat, but no arrangement has as yet been made.
Are there fishermen who own steamers available for this purpose ?

No, the arrangement will have to be made with the people who are in the steamship business.
Miscellaneous-to pay Wm. Perkins for extra copies of evidence in connection with the Lisgar election petition, $80.36.
What is this for ?

The Order in Council providing for copies of evidence taken at election trials makes provision for the payment of ten cents a folio for the first copy and three cents a folio for each additional copy. In this particular instance there was no copy required by the judges and the only copy taken was the copy furnished to Mr. Speaker. The Auditor General in construing the Order in Council came to the conclusion that Mr. Perkins was only entitled to three cents a folio. Strictly speaking that is correct. We have amended the Order in Council so as to make provision that if the stenographer is only required to make one copy he is entitled to ten cents a folio. In view of the fact that this' work was done before the Order in Council was passed, it is necessary to get parliamentary authority to pay this sum.
How does it come that the Dominion ought to pay any sum at all for election trials ?

Election courts are federal courts. All the expenditure at the trial of an election petition in connection with an election to the Dominion parliament is under our control, and we are absolutely responsible for it. The question was formerly raised in the case of Valin vs. Langlois, as to whether judges of the provincial courts can try election cases and the point was finally decided by the Privy Council to the effect that judges of the provincial courts sitting for the purpose of trying federal cases are federal judges.
Surely they would make the orders and rules sufficiently binding to provide themselves with a copv of the petition.

This is not to provide for a copy of the petition. This is for a copy of the evidence taken at the trial. The stenographer took the notes of the evidence for which he was paid, but when the notes are extended, provision is made that they shall be paid for at so much per folio for each copy made. In this case the judge did not deem it necessary for the purpose of preparing their judgment to have the notes extended but it was necessary for the return to have a copy of the evidence sent here and it is for the copy of the evidence furnished to Mr. Speaker that we are asking for this vote.
Further amount required for printing Dominion notes. $30,000.

Hon. gentlemen have expressed the wish, that the notes should be as clean as possible, and as the circulation is increasing rapidly we find it necessary to come to the House and ask for this increased amount.
Do you take up the old' note ?

As rapidly as the bank sends us in old notes, we replace them with new ones ; it costs us a little more but I am sure the House will appreciate it.
To pay Lady Lafontaine a pension at the rate' of $1,800 per annum from January 1, 1903, $2,700.

This vote is required to pay a pension to the widow of Sir Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine. whose memory is revered in Canada. Sir Louis Lafontaine died in 1863. leaving a widow who was his second wife. When she married Sir Louis Lafontaine'. she was the' widow of an officer who had served in the garrison of Montreal. She was a Mrs. Kimpton ; her family name being Morrison. Lady Lafontaine was left, not in affluence, but in fairly comfortable circumstances ; and through reverses, she has been unfor-
tuniately reduced, to a state of absolute penury- Lady Lafontaine is now 82 years of age, and I am sure everybody will agree that this is the right thing to do.

Carried.
Expenses in connection with the conversion of the public debt. Payments may he made to members of the civil service, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service or Superannuation Acts. $5,000.

We have very large sums of old debts maturing this year, and to provide for their payment, and to make arrangements for replacing them with new loans so far as may be necessary, will involve some considerable negotiation in London, and probably several visits to that centre of the money market of the world. The deputy minister has been in England for some considerable time ; he has left to return home, but no doubt it will be necessary later on for some one to go there again. A considerable part of this item will be necessary for travelling expenses. The balance is in order to make provision for a change in the Finance Department, which I can hardly say I desire to make, but which I will be obliged, to make. The deputy minister, who has occupied his position with great satisfaction to all parties for many years, has expressed a desire to retire, and I am making arrangements to supply his place. At the same time, in view of the very large financial operations which are to be undertaken during the current year and for the next year or two, I am anxious that we should retain Mr. Courtney's services in an advisory capacity. I deem it wise that we should have some such officer, and I shall have to take a portion of this money to apply it to the payment of Mr. Courtney in addition to the superannuation he would be entitled to receive. It is a mere temporary arrangement for a year or two, so that we may have the benefit of his services during this period when so much financing has to be done. Mr. Courtney is now on the ocean, and as it is a matter of arrangement with him I am not able to say how much we will pay him.
The law provides that you can take a superannuated officer back into the service at the same salary which he had when he retired ; you will not pay him more than that.

I do not expect we will allow him that much. We would not wish to recall Mr. Courtney back into the service to dischaige the duties of a deputy ; we do not want two deputies. He wishes to be relieved of the ordinary labour and responsibility of the department, but we want to retain him in an advisory capacity with regard to this special business and of course he will be valuable in instructing the new deputy minister on coming into
office. The idea is to give Mr. Courtney something supplementary to his superannuation, for a year or two years.

This does not relieve him from the responsibility of having his accounts audited by the Auditor General;
I think he got into some trouble with the Auditor General about his travelling expenses.
That trouble was based upon a difficulty which arose in the time of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) when exactly a similar case occurred, and we followed the precedent.
There are some precedents you should avoid.

The Auditor General, who above all things wishes to be consistent, thought that as he objected to a similar case under the administration of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart), he ought to do likewise in our case.
What is the aggregate of the sums falling due this year ?
The amount is stated to be $33,512,000.	,
Yes; that is correct.
Has the Minister of Finance any unused borrowing powers ?

We have the standing power to renew existing loans.
Department of Secretary of State-to provide for three additional junior second-class clerkships, $2,100.

Two of these are now extra clerks, and it is pro*

posed to put them on the permanent list. The work was largely increased in the department owing to the Naturalization Act. The Secretary of State has pointed out to me. that while the expenditure in 1893 was $50,160, the present expenditure is $48,560, which shows a substantial reduction. At the same time, the revenue has increased from $12,400 to $52,000.
If you promote these two clerks, you should strike out the vote for fheir salaries from the ordinary expenditure.
These extra clerks will be included in the contingencies, whieh have already been voted. It must be the intention that these items should not be used for the extra clerks.
Why do you not strike it out of the other vote ?

It has been already voted-, and this item, is necessary in order to make these gentlemen permanent.
Department of Justice-to increase the salaries of A. Power, K.C., and G. L. B. Fraser, K.C., by $200 each, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $400.
Is this their annual increase ?

No. These two gentlemen are both first-class clerks in the department. One has been there since 1874 and the other since 1879. They are now in receipt of salaries in excess of the statutory allowance. Each is receiving $2,600, and it is proposed to give them each $2,800. They are both very competent officials, and this is to give them some recognition for the valuable services they render.
To increase the salary of Miss M. Quain to $500, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $100.

Miss Quain is a stenographer. She gets a salary of $400, and is entitled to an annual increase of only $30. The result is that she says she will not remain at that salary. She is a very competent person, and I find that to retain competent officials you must pay them.
To increase \he salary of A. J. McGillivray, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $50.

He is from the maritime provinces. He has been in the department, I think, since 1890, and has never been put on the permanent list. He gives great satisfaction. Two first-class clerks have left the department and I am not going to replace them now, and I think Mr. McGillivray is entitled to this increase. He now gets $700.
To provide for employment of Thomas Morris as temporary clerk at $600, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $600.

In what we call the docket office we had a first-class clerk in Mr. Blakadar, who died some time ago. Mr. Morris is a man who is over age to come under the Civil Service Act, but he had a long experience in a lawyer's office in town and came to me highly recommended. He is a man of considerable attainments as a managing clerk, and is just the sort of man I wanted.
Office of the Auditor General-to promote B. W. Sherwood. W. Tucker, S. S. Allen and E. S. Johnston to the second class, $800, less $512.50 available from total sum included in main estimates. $287.50.
Did these parties pass the civil service examination ?

I think all the officials of the Auditor General have Mr. SPROULE.
passed the civil service examination. He has the right of promotion under the statute.

I have no objection whatever to_ this vote, but I think there are other clerks in that office who should be included in this promotion. I have in mind one clerk in particular, who has performed very efficient and very faithful service-D. J. -Wagner. I would suggest that the minister make inquiry and find out why he has not been included in the promotion granted to his fellow clerks ?

My hon. friend is invading the holy of holies. That is a privilege which I would not presume to exercise. The Auditor General has the right under the statute to promote the clerks of his department. I would not dare to question his judgment. He may be right or he may be wrong ; - but we must bow our heads submissive.

Notwithstanding the opinion of the hon. Minister of Finance that the Auditor General has power under the statute to promote, I know that some of the predecessors of the Minister of Justice held that notwithstanding the statute you could not interfere with the prerogative of the Crown-that the appointment is with the government, and that they are responsible for it.

In view of my hon. friend's statement as a public man of long experience, and in view of the fact that he quotes the authority of eminent Ministers of Justice, perhaps we shall have to consider the matter and see whether we have not the right.
I would suggest that a good opportunity for exercising that right would be the promotion of Mr. Wagner.

I understood the Auditor General to intimate that he was short of hands in his department. The complaint was made at the time the report was got out. I think he stated in the Public Accounts Committee that if be had more hands he could get it out earlier. Has the Minister of Finance looked into that at all ?
I have heard complaints that his department is very cramped.

In that respect I think he has some cause for complaint. The whole Finance Department is very much cramped. The other ministers have been more energetic and have got mew buildings, but because of my modesty I have not succeeded in getting any.
Supreme Court-to .provide salary of E. R. A. Taschereau, $1,200.

This is in connection with the revision of the statutes. The ex-Chief Justice of the Supreme Court was appointed chairman and he brought his .secretary with him. During his absence Mr. Taschereau, son of the Chief Justice, acted as secretary.
The former secretary is not receiving any additional salary ?

No.
To assist L. W. -Coutllee in publication of digest of judgments of Supreme Court of Canada, $500.

Mr. Coutlee is one of the reporters of the Supreme Court. He has taken upon himself the publication of a rather valuable work, and the practice has been to give assistance to those who publish books of that sort.
Further amount required for miscellaneous expenditure including North-west Territories, $5,000.

In the main estimates we have asked for $37,000, and this will make the total $42,000. The expenses there have grown enormously in the last ten years. The number of criminal cases tried has increased from 353 in 1891 to 3,296. The fees for juries and witnesses have increased from $3,240 to $11,000. It will be soon time to consider whether or not we could not place the administration of criminal justice under control of the local authorities. By the Act we have made provision to hand over to them the administration of civil justice.
Give them provincial autonomy.

They will soon be ready for that.
To provide salary for an additional judge of the Supreme Court of the North-west Territories, $4,000.

In the territories we are responsible entirely for the administration of justice, and the business has increased enormously. We have had demands from all over the territories, especially from the Macleod district, for additional judges. It was suggested that we should appoint two, but I made inquiry and found that one would be quite sufficient.
Wbo is going to fill the position, and where will he be stationed ?

I have really never thought of that. In the amendments to the North-west Territoiries Act we are giving to the local assembly the division of the districts and the arrangements of the works.
To provide salary for a junior judge of the district of Nipissing, Ont., $2,000.

That is one of the cases In which the Ontario legislature provide for the appointment. After making inquiries, I found that the district is a growing one and that one judge, even if he did not do much more than travel around, would have very little time to try the cases.
It seems an anomaly that this parliament -could not have the fixing of the district and the number of judges when we have to provide the salaries.

The remedy is in our own hands. We need not give the salary. The reason for the appointment is that, under the Ontario statute, where there is a certain population in the district, they are entitled to a senior and junior judge. Does this come up to the population ?

I am-assuming that the Ontario legislature has taken all these matters into account. I follow the principle laid down by the late Sir John A. Macdonald, and concurred in by the present Prime Minister, that the responsibility for the administration of civil justice is' with the province, and, if the province in the exercise of its authority says that it is necessary in the interest of litigants that a judge should be appointed for a certain place we-though, in the abstract we have the power-are not to interfere with the discretion on -the part of the province.
Can the hon. minister say what the limit of population is.
I think it is 80,000.
For 80,000 and over they might have a junior and senior judge, but for less than that only one.
Is this a junior judge ?
Yes.
This comprises more than the district of Nipissing ?
It is a group of constituencies.

The district, I think, is large enough.

1426a
And rather difficult for a judge to get about in, I should fancy.

I think the appointment is a proper one, as the district is large and an inconvenient one to cover. I was going to say, with regard to the other point, that the Ontario legislature some time ago, passed a law providing that where a district was below 80,000 it should be entitled to only one judge. That was when the Conservative party was in power at Ottawa, and it was said to be to prevent the appointment of more judges by that government. But when the Reform party came into power, the legislature repealed that law, and it is no longer in force.

I was under the impression that it still existed.
To raise the salary of the judge of the county court for district No. 7, Nova Scotia, to $3,000, $600.

The hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler) will understand this item. Judge Dodd is the judge of district No. 7, Nova Scotia, which includes Sydney. It appears that the business at Sydney has increased enormously of recent years, and I find, on examination, that the amount of business done at Sydney is even very much greater than at Halifax, and the intention is to provide a salary equal to that paid at Halifax.
Mr. FOWLER, What constituencies does this district No. 7 include ?
Victoria, Cape Breton and Richmond.
The salary is the same as paid at St. John ?
The same as paid at St. John, Halifax and Charlottetown.

I do not object to the- judge of district No. 7 receiving an increase, but I believe very strongly that the other judges of the county court of Nova Scotia, should be increased also. The reason alleged for the increase is that a great deal more work is done in district No. 7 than, any other district. I do not wish to be understood as doubting the accuracy of that statement. But if the judge there performs more work, it is only within the last year or two. Up to the year 1900 he did not perform anything like the amount of work done in district No. 3, or district No. 5. This matter was brought up in the local legislature of Halifax, and I have here the record of the debate which took place at the time and the remarks of Hon. Mr. Pipes, who was the leader of the legislative council in that province. That record shows that Judge Morse, of district No. 5, performed nearly double the work done by Judge Dodd of district No. 7.
Would' the hon. gentleman (Mr. Copp) kindly give details ?

District No. 5 includes the constituencies of Cumberland and Pictou. In 1900 the fees collected in Cumberland alone amounted to $365.85, or more than those of the whole district composed of Cape Breton, Victoria and Richmond, which amounted to $361.25. Besides this the-county of Pictou, which forms part ot district No. 5, collected fees to the amount of $224.80. This made a total for district No. 5 of $590.65, against $361.25 for district No. 7. Now. take the next district, district No. 4. We find that Judge Chipman, of that district performed nearly three times as much work as the judge of'district No. 7.
That is, received three times as large fees ?

Yes, that is the only guide we can have. The clerks of the county courts in Nova Scotia make a yearly return of the business done in their offices, and the debate to which I refer shows the figures given by these returns. In district No. 4 which includes the constituencies of Colchester, Hants and King's the fees were much larger than those of district No. 7. The fees in Colchester alone amounted to $439.50 or nearly $100 more than in the whole of district No. 7. In Hants, the fees were $233, and in King's $173. This made a total for the district of $846, against $361.25 for district No. 7. I am quoting from the figures given by Hon. Mr. Pipes who opposed this matter in the local legislature where it was discussed, but not in the form in which it now comes before us. It was proposed to divide district No. 7 and make one district of Cape Breton alone, leaving Richmond and Victoria to form a separate district, and to appoint a new judge. I think it is only fair to the other county court judges of Nova Scotia that I should read what Hon. Mr. Pipes had to say in reference to this very matter in 1901:
Hon. Mr. Pipes said a Bill had been before the Committee on Law and Amendments for some time to create an additional county clerk district. The committee was of the opinion that the necessity for this Bill had not been shown, and recommended that its further consideration, be deferred for three months. At the present time there were seven county court districts in the province. This Bill proposed to make eight. District No. 6 comprised the counties of Anti-gonish, Guysborough and Inverness.
And I wish to show that in the counties of Antigonish, Guysborough and Inverness the business was a great deal more than In district No. 7; the fees were $47&-in the-one, whereas they were $361 in district No. 7, or $100 more in district No. 6 than in district No. 7.
No. 7 comprised Cape Breton, Victoria and Richmond. The Bill proposed to make these two districts into three. If it passed the county
What do they receive ?
They receive $2,400.
That is the same as in Ontario.

The judges were appointed in 1870, and the salary was then fixed. The jurisdiction was also fixed at that time, but since then there has been a decided change in that respect. In 1880 the Speedy Trials Act was passed, which adds most materially to the duties of county court judges in Nova Scotia, owing to the fact that they have, under certain circumstances and for certain offences the power of trying criminal cases. Again, they are now masters of the Supreme Court, and they have large duties to perform as judges of probate. The old judges of probate in Nova Scotia have been done away with and these duties fall on the shoulders of the county court judges.
Do they not get fees for this work ?

No. Owing to these changes the duties of the county court judges of Nova Scotia have been more than doubled
since they were first appointed in 1876, but the salary has remained the same.
What becomes of the-probate fees ?

They go to the registrar of the court, who is paid by fees. In Nova Scotia they used to have a judge and registrar both, but now the duties are performed by the county court judges. I am quite sure that the duties performed by Judge Savary, one of the ablest judges in the province of Nova Scotia, an ornament to the bench, a man of high legal attainments, although his duties were not referred to by Mr. Pipes, must be equal to the duties of Judge Morse or Judge Chipman, and I am quite positive that they are- more onerous than the duties performed by the judge in district No. 7.
How-many cases did be try last year?

I do not know that, I have not the record. What I am asking is that this matter should be so dealt with that the cases of the other judges would also be considered by the minister. If this judge is entitled to an increase in salary, I say that Judge Morse in No. 5, Judge Chipman in No. 4, and Judge MeGillivray, who succeeded the late Judge Mclsaac in No. 0, should certainly have received larger salaries. The business in district No. 7 has not been anything like the business done by the other judges. While I do not object to this judge receiving an increase in his salary, I think it would be better if increases had been given to all the judges and not to this one alone. I have here the statistics up to 1900 of the amount of business done by the different judges. The minister states that the business of the judge for district No. 7 has increased, and that he performs more work than the judge of district No. 1. That may be true, but I would like to know what is the amount of business iu Halifax. I am very doubtful if the judge in Halifax does anything like the amount of business done in Colchester, Hants and King's. What we want to know is this : Is the judge of district No. 7 at the present time performing more duties than are the judges of the other county courts; I am very doubtful if he is; I am quite positive in my own mind that he is not. Take the probate business in the large county of Cumberland and Pictou. Take the business done as master of the Supreme Court; take the criminal business or the civil business done by the judge of district No. 5 in these two large counties, and I think you will find it largely exceeds the amount of business done by the county court judge in district No. 1. The mere fact that he is performing more work than the judge of district No. 1, the city of Halifax, is no guide for us that he should receive an increase in salary in preference to Judge

Morse, Judge Savary, Judge Chipman, and the other two judges to whom I have referred.
How do the populations compare as between the different districts ?

The population of district No. 7, including the counties of Cape Breton, Victoria and Richmond, is 73,246 ; district No. 5, including the counties of Cumberland and Pictou, 69,627 ; district No. 6, including the counties of Inverness, Guysborough and Antigonish, 56,290 ; district No. 3, including the counties of Digby, Yarmouth and Annapolis, 62,033 ,* district No. 4, including the counties of Colchester, King's and Hants, 66,893, showing that there is not much difference in population. To show that we cannot be guided altogether by population, I may say that the population of Halifax is 74,662, or nearly 10,000 more than the population of district No. 7. Mr. Pipes says that there is more business done in districts Nos. 4, 5 and 6 than in district No. 7. It is claimed that the duties of the judge of district No. 7 are largely increased. I want to say to the committee that the judge of district No. 7 is not performing more onerous duties than those which are performed by other judges, and it would appear to me to be only fair to the other judges that their salaries should be increased so as to bring them to the same level as that of the judge of district No.
7.	Hon. gentlemen know perfectly well that the judge of the county court does not do all the business of the county. To-day there are a large number of criminals in the jail at Sydney who are going to be tried by the Supreme Court and not by the county court judge.
Why should they be ?

Because criminals can only be tried by the county judge who are actually in the custody of the sheriff, and then they have the right to elect. Therefore, the number of criminals to be tried cannot show us the extent of the business that is done by the county court judge. I think it would be well for the hon. minister to secure from the different county court clerks a statement of the amount of business performed in each district in Nova Scotia, and then he will have something reliable to go upon. It will be found that these other judges have been performing for the last twenty years double the amount of business that the judge of district No. 7 has been performing, for which they have not been paid extra, and still he has been receiving the same salary as they have. It does seem rather strange that he should receive an increase of salary and that the others should remain at the same salary.

I think the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Copp) has made out such a strong case that the hon. Minister of Justice will move at once to strike out this
item. I do not see how he can defend the item after the argument which has been so ably made by the hon. member for Digby. I think he has proved that several judges of the county court are performing more onerous duties than those which are performed by the judge of district No. 7. I do not see why this judge should be distinguished from the others, nor do I see why he should receive more salary than the county court judges in New Brunswick. There are no junior judges there. Each judge has to perform the duties of the district to which he is appointed, and the same argument which the hon. member for Digby has applied in respect to the increased duties that are thrust upon these judges applies to the judges of New Brunswick as well. So that if the salary is increased in Nova Scotia it must be increased in New Brunswick. Until some uniform scale is adopted in respect to the judges of these provinces, I think it would be well to leave Judge Dodd at his old salary of $2,400.

My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Copp) has made out quite a strong case. He has been content to make reference to something that Mr. Pipes said in the Nova Scotia legislature in 1900, about statistics but that does not seem to be very conclusive because he discussed the amount of fees received by the clerks of the court. I have something a little better than that, and I think a little more conclusive. In Halifax the judge gets $3,000 a year. I find that in Halifax last year there were 35 speedy trials, 31 civil cases, and 87 applications in chambers disposed of, whereas, in Sydney, the speedy trials numbered 21, civil cases, 158, and chamber applications disposed of 354. So that, you will see that there is three or four times more work done in Sydney than in Halifax. I have not taken the trouble to make inquiry in respect to the other districts that my hon. friend has referred to, but this is a comparative statement between Halifax, which I thought was the most important judicial centre of Nova Scotia, and Sydney. My hon. friend must not imagine that Sydney has remained stationary. Sydney lias been increasing in population and importance and in the last few years, as busi-iness has increased, the judicial necessities of the place have also increased. I have given my hon. friend the result of the comparison between the two places showing that there is four times as much business done at Sydney as at Halifax.
I do not know that that is a fair test to apply as to salary.

If you start in and say it is fair to give a judge at Halifax $3,000 a year, surely you cannot dispute the correctness of the proposition that a judge who does four times the work is at least entitled to the same salary.
That may be true, but why should the judge at Halifax get more than the judges in the rural districts ?
My hon. friend must ask my predecessor that.

Your predecessor is not here. If he were here my hon. friend would not be occupying that position. The judge of a rural district has to devote all his time to the performance of his judicial duties. He can do nothing else. He has no other way of earning a living, except by acting as judge. He does all the business that is brought before him, and he should be entitled to the same remuneration for all his time as a judge who does more business. It seems to me that if I were a county court judge I should prefer, even at the same salary, to be a judge in one of those districts in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; they have all they can do to keep themselves out of mischief, or perhaps I should say, idleness. Their duties are not very heavy on the bench, and I think there should be a uniform scale of remuneration for judges whether the judge lives in the city or in the country. It may be that his living expenses would be greater by living in a city like Halifax than in Sydney, and I say that with all respect to my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall). Sydney, I fancy, is not as expensive a place to live in as Halifax.
Much more so.
Even if there should be a little more business in one place than another there should be no discrimination amongst the judges.
I think that is right.
I think the hon. minister will do well to strike out this item.
It will not prevent an increase to the other judges; on the contrary, the tendency always has been to level up the others, not to level down.
Will the minister promise to look into the business done by the other judges ?
I will not give any undertaking ; to depreciate one does not help the other.

Although I have listened to the criticism with a great deal of interest, I think the proper view is that we had better let this $600 be voted because it will form a reason for increasing the salaries of the other judges. There is no doubt that the salaries of the county court judges are more deserving to be raised than the salaries of Supreme Court judges in Nova Scotia. A man is not badly off with a salary of $4,000, and travelling expenses, to the extent of
$1,000, which practically means a salary of $4,800 or $5,000 a year. A county court judge in Nova Scotia does more work than most of the Supreme Court judges as a rule; and while $4,000 is a fair salary, with the addition of the circuit indemnity, the salary given to the county court judge is absolutely penurious. The salary of the Supreme Court judge will keep him in decency and enable him to show some moderate style of hospitality ; but a county court judge with a salary of $2,400, is required to maintain about the same social position, and while the one has a salary of $5,000 a year, the other has to skimp along with $2,400, and it becomes almost unendurable. I know Judge Dodd very well; he is a very capable man.
I believe he is one of the most competent judges we have.

He is a capable man all round. He was a member of this House; he belongs to a distinguished judicial family in Nova Scotia ; his father was an eminent judge in our province, and I do not begrudge him his addition to his salary. Take the case of Judge Morse, at Amherst. He refused a Supreme Court judgeship some years ago. because he had a large establishment in Cumberland county requiring his personal attention and did not wish to leave Amherst. He Is a very eminent man in Nova Scotia, and to offer such a man $2,400 a year is an indignity. I say that the salary of the Nova Scotia county court judges ought to be raised, in preference to any other judicial salaries in Nova Scotia. I want to put myself on record on that score, because we have very capable men as county court judges. They were all good lawyers, enjoying a good practice, men of good ability ; men like Dodd and Morse, eminent men, far above the average lawyer we have in Nova Scotia.
That is saying a good deal.

Yes it is. We have had quite a run of big fish down there. The breed is a little run out just now, but we hope to improve it. There is too much difference between the salary of a county-court judge at $2,400, and a Supreme Court judge at $5,000.
Do they not act as local judges of the Supreme Court ?

I am not of the legal profession, but I am able to say that during the last three or four years the work of Judge Dodd has been very onerous indeed. The population of the district over which he has jurisdiction is not 73,000, but probably 87,000. We have had come to us, amongst the great influx of population, a large element that gives rise to a considerable amount of legal work. To my knowledge, Judge Dodd spends the greater part [DOT]of his time discharging his duties, and no man of his attainments should be expected to work continuously as he does, for a salary of $2,400. I certainly think that $3,000 is little enough for the position that he occupies.

I do not wish to be understood as being opposed to this increase of salary for Judge Dodd. I believe that he is entitled to it. But I contend that the county court judges should receive the same increase.

When you are taking into [DOT]consideration the raising of the salaries of the Nova Scotia county court judges, you must not forget an equally able body of men: the county court judges of New Brunswick, who perform just as arduous duties as do their confreres in Nova Scotia.

The salaries of all the judges throughout Canada will have to be considered together.
Yukon law library, $2,000.
There was money voted for this last year.

Like the poor, we always have these expenditures with us.
M. FOWLER. Who buys these books ?
The request is sent by the judges, to the department. It is checked over by us, and the order is given over by the deputy minister.
Do you have a central library at Dawson ?

Yes. When a judicial district in a territory is first established we provide the law library until the Bar Association is formed to take it over. Last year the Regina law library was taken over by the Regina Law Association, which will he responsible for it in the future. When the cost of freight is added, these books cost a very large sum in the Yukon. The judges have no access to public libraries, and as the cases are of considerable importance, we must supply them with law books. I hope that next year the Yukon Bar will be sufficiently important to take over the library. Including this vote we have spent altogether about $12,000.
Do the judges all reside at Dawson ?
Yes, the only other place at which they occasionally hold court is at White Horse.
This is a large item coming year after year. It is doubtful if we use that much for the library here.

I ventured to suggest this year that we should send up the old editions of our text books which we have at the Supreme Court, where ws are constantly renewing our library by putting in new editions. With a few exceptions, the old editions are as good as the new. Often a man issues a new edition simply to sell it. My suggestion was protested against, but I have made up my mind that we .should do that.
How much has been spent altogether on this library ?

This will make $12,000.
To pay the account ol the Prince Albert ' Advocate ' for announcing the proclamation and notice of the Saskatchewan election of 1900, notwithstanding anything in the Dominion Elections Act. $297.48.

Was the payment of this account not refused by the Auditor General ?
The PRIA1E A1INISTER. Yes.

The point was that it did not come within the schedule of services specially authorized ; but the view was taken that the exceptional circumstances justified the returning officer in publishing these notices.
Will this complete the payment of all the election expenses of the election of 1900 ?
No, I think not. There hare been some items standing for some time which have been the subject of negotiation with the Auditor General.
This seems an enormous sum of money for advertising the ordinary proclamation. In an ordinary city it costs only $15.

This item does not concern my constituency. Prince Albert is in tire constituency of Mr. Davis, the member for Saskatchewan, and I can merely tell the committee what he told me concerning this item when the supplementary estimates first came down. In order that the people may know the boundaries between the polling divisions, it is necessary that the proclamation setting forth the boundaries shall receive the fullest possible publication, because a man votes on residence, and is entitled to vote only in the polling division in which he resides. The population varying all the time by continual increase, ' the [DOT]boundaries are different from time to time.

In the Prince Albert district there is a mixed population of French and English, and it was thought desirable by the returning officer that the proclamation setting forth the boundaries of the polling divisions should be printed in the newspaper in French and English. It was so done, and this is the bill. I believe the payment has been delayed some considerable time on the ground, I suppose, that the bill was large.
The proclamation would be only three or four inches in length ?
No, it sets forth every polling division. I do not know how many there were in Saskatchewan, but in Alberta there were over eighty.
Is not the proclamation put up also ?

The law provides that the proclamation shall be posted up, but in Saskatchewan it was thought that was not sufficient and that it would be desirable to put it in the newspaper. The returning officer thought it was desirable to have the boundaries of the polling divisions printed in the newspapers.
I think the newspaper editor was kicking.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman why this should be necessary in the Saskatchewan county and not in his own ?

I do not know that it was really more necessary in the one than in the other. It was just a matter of opinion on the part of the returning officer. He did not consider that the posting of the proclamation gave sufficiently accurate publicity, and he thought of supplementing it by this means. I may say that even in the district of Alberta, the posting of the proclamation is found rather insufficient, and for my own part, I publish the boundaries of the polling divisions in my own locality, but I do not publish the boundaries throughout the whole district. That would be altogether too much. But I considered that the posting of the proclamation was insufficient. I felt that there was the same lack of information as was felt in this case, and I published the actual boundaries in the few districts where my paper is circulated.
Did you charge it to the government ?
No, I did not.
Is this a Tory paper ?
I could not say.

Was there an amount similar to this paid in connection with the election of 1896 ? I would suppose that if this was necessary in 1900, it would be more necessary in 1896, because the population would naturally then be less conversant with the boundaries of the different municipalities and the different polling sub-divisions. We should have some information why it is necessary to pay this amount in that one particular constituency when no such neces-city exists anywhere else.
I have no personal knowledge of the matter and we will let the item stand until I can get information from the Secretary of State.

My hon. friend lias said that as the population increases and becomes more established, the boundaries of the polling divisions will become better known. On the contrary, as the population increases the boundaries of the polling divisions have to be changed, and it is because of the continual changes from the increase of the population that it is desirable the fullest possible information should be given immediately before each election. It was for that reason I published the boundaries in my newspaper. The differences between the conditions in Alberta and Saskatchewan are these, Throughout Alberta there are a number of centres of settlements, each of which has its local paper. My paper, which is published in the north end of the constituency, does not circulate largely in the southern or central part. The papers published at Calgary have no large circulation at either end, and the southern papers have no large circulation at either the centre or the north ; but in the case of Prince Albert, that is the chief town of the Saskatchewan district, and the Prince Albert papers cover the whole district of the Saskatchewan. But the publisher of any paper in Alberta would not cover the whole district of Alberta.

Any one conversant with the Election Act must know that it gives no authority to the returning officer to do this. His duty is clearly set out, and the number of proclamations which shall he posted-three in each polling sub-division. These give all the information to which the voter is entitled, and it was a gratuitous act on the part of the returning officer to order this advertisement. I do not understand how the Attorney General allowed the item to pass. With regard to the charge, even though the publications were in French and English, $300 seems an exorbitant figure. I am afraid it was only a sop given some newspaper man, who perhaps either was a strong advocate of the member elected or one of these people who are

always desirous to get as much as possible out of an election.

No objection was taken by the Auditor General to the price, as not being fair and reasonable. The only objection he took was that the returning officer had no authority to do this. But after all lie was an officer of parliament and acted in good faith ; and, as the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) has explained, the posting of these publications does not give sufficient notice where so many new settlers are coming in, I am inclined to think that we should pass this item under the circumstance.

What the hon. minister has said would apply to every constituency in British Columbia, Manitoba and territories. They are all in a new country comparatively speaking, and the population is continually changing, but no returning officer, except in this constituency, has been so wanting in intelligence as not to keep within the law. It is just possible that between the returning officer and the proprietor of the paper, it was agreed that this advertisement should be put in on the chance of its being paid for.

I am not too particular about accounts, but I have a suspicion that this claim is a pure after-thought. This gentleman was a warm supporter of the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis). They published this matter, probably, as campaign matter. I know I spend several hundred dollars for campaign work in my own constituency, and I neither know nor care what it is for.
Probably for the other fellow.

I cannot bother with these things. But I am a little more frank in these matters than most people are. I do not see any use in being a hypocrite. Every one who runs an election knows what is done. It seems to me that in this case this was simply campaign work done in the interest of the candidate by the party paper.
It could not be campaign work. It was not partisan material.

It is necessary in the interest of the candidate that there should be full knowledge on the part of the people of the constituency as to the boundaries of polling subdivisions, so that his voters may go to the right place.
Both parties would have the advantage of this advertisement.

I know. But I can easily conceive circumstances under which this would be excellent campaign work. I do not think it should be paid for. It was probably published for the bene-Mr. SPROULE.
fit of the party, and afterwards some ingenious fellow developed the idea of sending the account into the government to see if they could get it through. I would rather vote ?1,000 that this man had honestly earned, than vote ten cents for an unjust claim.

Let it stand.
Item allowed to stand.
To pay arrears of superannuation rilowanees to ex-lockmaster W. J. Casselman, Williamsburg canals, from January 1, 1902, to June 30, 1903, at $97.37 per annum, $146.05 ; to increased allowance for year ending June 30, 1904 to $296.63 at which sum it shall hereafter be paid, $97.37, total' $243.42.

This is to correct an error in the superannuation. This gentleman had been a lockmaster and his services were dispensed with by bis superior. He was afterwards restored to duty, but not classed as a lockmaster. When superannuated later on, he was superannuated at a lower salary than that of a lock-master. On further Investigation, it was found that, in dispensing with his services, no Order in Council had been passed, and technically he had not ceased to be a lock-master, and so was entitled to superannuation on a lockmaster's salary.
Dominion lands-chargeable to income-further amount required for protection of timber and tree planting, $15,000.

Before I explain this item, I may say that I was asked by one of the hon. gentlemen on the other side a question with regard to the printing of maps. I have here the information about that. I am informed that with reference to the question In the House as to the purchase of maps by the Geological Survey, the usual course Is pursued by the Geological Survey of forwarding all requisitions to the King's Printer, and the maps are purchased by that officer. I understand they are all supplied in Canada, some having been bought from the Burland Company, others from Mortimer & Co., Ottawa, the Federal Press Company, and also the Toronto Lithographing Company.

None from the United
States ?
No, we would not go to the United States.
I suppose the prices are reasonable ?
I have no reason to doubt It.

Were they produced in>
Canada or only purchased here ?

I could not say. As to this item with regard to protection of timber and tree-planting, I was asked to give some information of what had

been done by the department this year. I find that 22 forest fire rangers were employed during the dry weather; eight in the railway belt in British Columbia, six in the North-west Territories, and eight in Manitoba. Also 8,790 fire notices on parchment were posted along the routes of travel warning the public against careless use of fire. In addition to this, over 5,000 circulars were distributed and a large number of copies of the Bush Fires Act of British Columbia, the Prairies Fires Ordinance of the North-west Territories, and the Fire Prevention Act of Manitoba have been circulated. Fire-guards at Banff and on the west side of the Turtle Mountain timber reserve have been constructed. The Long lake timber reserve has been explored and set aside, also the Yoho park and the Bocky Mountains park greatly enlarged. Since the adoption of the fire-ranging system we have practically lost no timber in the railway belt in British Columbia, notwithstanding two very dry seasons.
As to tree-planting on the plains, the officers of the department advise me that, in co-operation with the settlers, 918,000 seedling trees and 564 pounds of tree seed were planted. These were given free to farmers last year, the average of trees to each farmer being about 1,450. The report of the inspector is that about 80 per cent of the trees sent out that have gone through the winter are still living, and that about 90 per cent of last year's planting were living last fall. This spring 630 settlers received trees, and the number of new applicants for trees for next season is 1,649. We have set apart a reserve for tree-planting at Indian Head, and the vote is to provide also for that. There is increase!? work in guarding timber. This item will include additional fire rangers at forestry station at Indian Head and additional buildings.

The right hon. gentleman left the question of the maps unfinished. I would like to ask if the maps were printed in Canada. I am under the impression that they were printed in the United States, though I may be wrong. I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that some were supplied by the Burland Company. I take it that they would be lithographed in Canada. There were some also by an Ottawa firm.

Mortimer & Co. They are engravers and lithographers, and have done work for the government for many years. They have done work also for the Post Office Department, and are very reliable officers. The firm in Toronto is also a very large lithographing firm. It is a house that would make such maps as this. I have no knowledge of this item, but I think we may fairly assume that this is their work. That company did some engraving for the Post Office Department, 447
in making maps of some of the provinces, so that I know they do that class of work.
In the committee it came out that the small atlases that have been so generally circulated in Canada and the United States were produced in the United States.

I think the only thing wie can do is to have reciprocity in this matter and to exact a promise from the Postmaster General that if we allow this to pass he will not be so belligerent in reference to our mail bags.
To compensate the Canadian Bank of Commerce for services in the Yukon, from May 1, 1902 to April 30, 1903. $19,000.

This is a vote to pay the Bank of Commerce a commission on the business they handle in the Yukon. We have been reducing the percentage from year to year and after a short time affairs in the Yukon will get down to the same order as affairs throughout Canada, and we will not have any commission to pay. We paid the bank in the first year three-fourths of one per cent, in the second year we reduced it to five-eighths of one per cent, and for this year we have reduced it to one-half of one per cent.
This is based on the one-half of one per cent.
Yes.
Is this another case where Cox won't wait ?

No, in this case, so far as I know, they have enough faith to wait patiently.
To pay Charles Miller, $3,713.32 and Robert Miller, $3,339.05 for amounts deposited by them in the Post Office Savings Bank at St. Scholas-tique and fraudulently withdrawn by the assistant postmaster, $7,052.37.
Portions of moneys handed to the assistant postmaster of this town for deposit in the Post Office Savings Bank were appropriated by him for his own purposes.
What evidence have you that the money was deposited ?
The case went through the courts and the man is now serving his term in the penitentiary for it. The assistant postmaster who committed the thefts and forgeries had different methods of embezzling.
Was nothing recovered from him ?

He had nothing whatever. He was a member of a highly respectable family and his father, I think, had been the postmaster there for



u great many years. It was a very sad case.
Had he no bonds ?
Not for such a large amount as this ; he was, I think, covered by the insurance system hut the largest amount insured is very much less than this.
Was that paid ?

The amount paid out of our own fund, would not cover $7,000. We have in the Post Office Department a system of insurance by assessment upon the staff. Each postmaster is assessed a certain sum and that assessment is put into a fund which is available to the extent that it is supposed to insure him. But we do not assess a man sufficiently to provide insurance to the amount of thousands of dollars. The amount of insurance for postmasters is comparatively small.

This opens a grave dif-iiculty. In Truro, for instance, there is an enormous amount deposited in the savings bank, and I would ask if there is no security for the public. Is not the custodian guaranteed by any security ?

I was explaining that there are a large number of the employees in the post office service, postmasters and persons in fiduciary positions, upon whom an assessment is levied. For instance, formerly when a man was appointed, he would give the bond of a trust company for $500 or $000, which was considered a large amount. He would pay this guarantee company an annual fee and they would issue a bond in his favour. In case of loss, if you could bring the loss within the terms of the bond, you would recover from that company the amount of that bond, but any shortage above this would of course be lost, unless he had property. Of late years the system has been changed and instead of taking the bond of a company or of a private citizen the department makes an assessment on the employees. For example, if a postmaster had to give bonds for $500, instead of his paying that assessment to a guarantee company and getting the bond of that guarantee company he would pay that amount to the government.
What is the limit in regard to a deposit in the post office savings bank for one depositor V
I think any man can deposit $3,000 without a permit and above that he is obliged to have a permit.
That feature was considered in this case ?
I do not recall that point.
I observe that in one case the amount was $3,713.
These are very thrifty people. I think they are two brothers.
That is not my .point. My point is as to the amount of money they can deposit.
I think the amount includes interest.
1 have heard that the limit is $1,000.
I think it is $3,000.
The excess is probably the interest added.

$3,000 would meet my point. I think the lion. Postmaster General ought to be able to tell the committee the total amount that these depositors had at their credit because the House would naturally be required to vote the difference between that and the amount from that guarantee fund to which the hon. Postmaster General has referred out of which the defaulter would have a certain amount available to meet this defalcation and we should only be asked to vote the difference between that and the amount to which the depositor is entitled. What is that sum ?
If the hon. gentleman has not all these particulars the item should stand because as a matter of .business we ought to rote no more than the actual amount due.
This, I am assured, represents only the balance required after taking into account the sum received from the insurance fund.
I think this item should be allowed to stand.
In answer to my hon. and learned friend from Pictou (Hon. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) the hon. Postmaster General said that any one man could deposit $3,000.
The crime was not in respect to the $3,000. He cannot put in more than $1,000 in one year.
He can put that in in one day. Could any number of people deposit $1,000 with the Postmaster General in one day ?
Yes.
Then the lion., Postmaster General might he the recipient in one day of $100,000. How long does the postmaster keep that money ?
If there is a bank in the town he is obliged to deposit with the bank to the credit of the receiver general every day before the close of banking hours.
Then lie issues a pass book to the person making the deposit V
No, the pass book is issued at Ottawa by the savings bank department here.
He gives a receipt V
It strikes me that the system is rather loose, because the postmaster, if he is only required to give a receipt or issue a pass book, might receive an enormous amount of money.
He does not issue a pass book.

The people in the country have the utmost confidence in the Post Office Savings Bank system and there should be no slip. There has been a slip in this matter and when there has been a slip in this case it might occur in other cases unless there is something very peculiar about this case. I want to find out how this man did this ?
He forged the depositor's name.

In some instances he forged cheques and in other instances he simply embezzled money handed in for deposit. He would make an entry in the pass book, show it to these men then put it in his pocket and erase the entry. He carried on a system of frauds for a long time.
If we give too much information as to how this thing can be done we will make it easy.
The hon. Postmaster General said that he made an entry in this pass book and then erased it. That would be detected when it reached Ottawa.
I will get all the information in regard to the item.
We might have a large deposit made every day.
There need not be any want of confidence on the part of the public because 'the fact that we are voting this item shows that the public are protected.

But this is a matter *of grace. Suppose parliament did not vote this money what would these men do ?
447}
The government would be responsible. There is no question about that.
I do not suppose as a matter of law they could recover because this man has committed a crime.
Yes, they could recover. If a depositor hands in money to the postmaster he is the agent of the government and the government are therefore responsible for the money.

I think the hon. Minister of Justice would get up an ingenious defence and that he would take the ground that if an officer of the government did something outside of the government regulations the government could not be held responsible.

This is a very exceptional case. The man who was postmaster at this place was also notary and he was acting as agent for these men and a part of his fraud consisted in representing that he was investing their money for them.
